question.question: "Are mutations in DNA repair pathway genes (BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2) enriched in specific cancer types across TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas?"
question.notes: A correct answer must: compute per-cancer-type mutation frequency of BRCA1/BRCA2/ATM/CHEK2 in pan_cancer_tcga (e.g. gene_mutation_frequency_by_cancer_type) and note that hypermutated types (endometrial, colorectal MSI, melanoma) inflate frequencies; may hand off enrichment tests to group comparison. Must not: sum across studies or invent p-values.

reply.answer:
**Short answer:** Yes, in descriptive terms. Mutation frequencies in these four genes differ a lot between TCGA cancer types, but I haven't run a statistical test, so I can't say whether the differences are significant. The highest rates are in endometrial, melanoma, bladder, colorectal and esophagogastric tumors. These are mostly the same types that carry high overall mutation burdens.

**Cohort:** TCGA PanCancer Atlas, 32 studies grouped by cancer type. The unit is samples, with mutated samples divided by samples profiled for that gene. Only cancer types with at least 50 profiled samples are shown. Counts are mutations of any type, not filtered for driver status.

| Cancer type | BRCA1 | BRCA2 | ATM | CHEK2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Endometrial (n=574) | 8.2% (47) | 14.5% (83) | 17.6% (101) | 6.3% (36) |
| Melanoma (n=440) | 6.4% (28) | 11.6% (51) | 9.5% (42) | 1.1% (5) |
| Bladder (n=410) | 5.1% (21) | 9.8% (40) | 13.4% (55) | 2.4% (10) |
| Colorectal (n=534) | 3.0% (16) | 7.1% (38) | 13.1% (70) | 1.7% (9) |
| Esophagogastric (n=618) | 2.9% (18) | 7.3% (45) | 8.3% (51) | 1.5% (9) |
| Non-small cell lung (n=1050) | 3.9% (41) | 5.7% (60) | 7.2% (76) | 1.6% (17) |
| Cervical (n=291) | 4.8% (14) | 4.5% (13) | 3.8% (11) | 1.4% (4) |
| Head and neck (n=515) | 2.1% (11) | 4.1% (21) | 3.3% (17) | 0.8% (4) |
| Ovarian (n=523) | 3.4% (18) | 2.9% (15) | 1.9% (10) | 0.8% (4) |
| Breast (n=1066) | 2.5% (27) | 2.7% (29) | 2.3% (25) | 0.8% (9) |
| Prostate (n=494) | 0.2% (1) | 1.6% (8) | 4.0% (20) | none listed |
| Thyroid (n=490) | 0.2% (1) | 0.4% (2) | 1.2% (6) | 0.8% (4) |
| Glioma (n=514) | 0.4% (2) | 1.4% (7) | 0.8% (4) | 0.4% (2) |

Cancer types not listed for a gene had no mutated samples or fewer than 50 profiled samples. Pancreatic, adrenocortical and several other types also have lower-count rows that I left out of the table.

**Patterns**
- **Endometrial carcinoma** has the highest frequency for all four genes: ATM 17.6%, BRCA2 14.5%, BRCA1 8.2% and CHEK2 6.3%.
- **ATM** is the most frequently mutated of the four in most types. Bladder (13.4%) and colorectal (13.1%) follow endometrial.
- **BRCA2** is highest in endometrial, melanoma (11.6%) and bladder (9.8%).
- **CHEK2** is mutated at low rates everywhere, apart from endometrial (6.3%).
- **Breast and ovarian** tumors, the classic BRCA1/2 cancers, have fairly modest rates in this data (about 2–3%). Frequencies don't rise just because a cancer is known for BRCA-related predisposition.
- **Low-frequency types** include thyroid, prostate (except ATM), glioma and kidney clear cell.

**Caveats**
- **Hypermutated tumors:** Endometrial (POLE/MSI), melanoma, bladder, colorectal (MSI) and esophagogastric tumors carry many mutations overall. Large genes like ATM and BRCA2 pick up passenger mutations there. High frequency in these types may reflect mutation burden rather than DNA-repair-specific selection.
- **No driver filter:** This database has no driver annotation for TCGA, so I can't say which mutations are functionally relevant. In the portal you can apply the `MUT_DRIVER` OQL modifier to get OncoKB annotations.
- **No significance test:** To test enrichment formally, compare a type against all others with Fisher's exact test. You can do that in cBioPortal's Group Comparison, or in R with `fisher.test`. Use FDR correction across the four genes and many cancer types.
- **Lung types are merged:** Lung adenocarcinoma and squamous carcinoma are combined as "Non-small cell lung" in these groupings.

**Links**
- [Alteration frequencies by cancer type for BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM and CHEK2 (mutations only, all 32 TCGA PanCancer Atlas studies)](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/cancerTypesSummary?cancer_study_list=acc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cblca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cbrca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ccesc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cchol_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ccoadread_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cdlbc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cesca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cgbm_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Chnsc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ckich_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ckirc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ckirp_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Claml_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Clgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Clihc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cluad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Clusc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cmeso_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cov_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cpaad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cpcpg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cprad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Csarc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cskcm_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cstad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ctgct_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cthca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cthym_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cucec_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cucs_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cuvm_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&gene_list=BRCA1%3A+MUT%0ABRCA2%3A+MUT%0AATM%3A+MUT%0ACHEK2%3A+MUT&case_set_id=all)

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.
- **For "across cancer types" questions**, jump to the [Cross-Cancer-Type Mutation Frequency](#cross-cancer-type-mutation-frequency) section below — there is one correct recipe and several common wrong ones.

## Counting Unit: Samples vs Patients

Before answering any mutation count or frequency question, decide whether the unit is samples or patients and state that choice in the answer.

| User wording | Counting unit |
|--------------|---------------|
| "prevalence", "rate", "fraction of patients", "patients with", "how common is" | Patient-level: `COUNT(DISTINCT patient_unique_id)` |

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. The shape "altered/not altered × group A/group B" needs Fisher's exact + a defined direction (odds ratio < 1 with significant p). Without that test, the agent presents the table and stops. Descriptive phrasing is also a claim: "largely/mostly mutually exclusive", "rarely co-occur", "tend to co-occur" are forbidden without the test — point to cBioPortal's Mutual Exclusivity tab instead.

question.question: Which cancer types have the highest aneuploidy scores and how does this correlate with mutation burden across TCGA Pan-Cancer studies?
question.expected_answer: Across TCGA Pan-Cancer studies, tumors with the highest aneuploidy burdens included seminoma, non-seminomatous germ cell tumor, adrenocortical carcinoma, non–small cell lung cancer, and bladder cancer, all of which displayed elevated median aneuploidy scores. Although bladder cancer and non–small cell lung cancer also ranked among the tumor types with the highest mutational burdens, seminoma and non-seminomatous germ cell tumors showed some of the lowest TMB values, with adrenocortical carcinoma exhibiting intermediate levels. These patterns indicate that aneuploidy does not reliably coincide with high mutation loads across tumor types.

reply.answer:
# Aneuploidy score vs. mutation burden across TCGA PanCancer Atlas

I used 32 TCGA PanCancer Atlas cohorts, with 9,975 samples that have both an aneuploidy score and a TMB value. TMB is the nonsynonymous tumor mutational burden in mutations per Mb. The counting unit is samples.

## Cancer types ranked by aneuploidy score

| Rank | Cancer type | n | Median aneuploidy | Mean aneuploidy | Median TMB | Mean TMB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Uterine Carcinosarcoma (UCS) | 56 | 19 | 17.2 | 1.55 | 4.32 |
| 2 | Testicular Germ Cell (TGCT) | 149 | 19 | 18.8 | 0.40 | 0.49 |
| 3 | Adrenocortical (ACC) | 89 | 17 | 18.3 | 0.90 | 2.83 |
| 4 | Lung Adenocarcinoma (LUAD) | 501 | 16 | 15.0 | 6.87 | 10.24 |
| 5 | Lung Squamous (LUSC) | 479 | 16 | 16.2 | 7.73 | 9.51 |
| 6 | Esophageal (ESCA) | 162 | 14.5 | 14.6 | 3.65 | 5.08 |
| 7 | Kidney Chromophobe (KICH) | 65 | 14 | 14.9 | 0.67 | 1.09 |
| 8 | Bladder (BLCA) | 400 | 14 | 13.6 | 5.90 | 8.57 |
| 9 | Ovarian (OV) | 504 | 13 | 14.0 | 1.90 | 2.26 |
| 10 | Colorectal (COADREAD) | 529 | 12 | 12.3 | 3.50 | 13.02 |

**Lowest aneuploidy (median):**
- Thyroid (THCA), AML (LAML) and Thymoma (THYM) each have a median of 0.
- Prostate (PRAD) has a median of 1.
- Lower-grade glioma (LGG) has a median of 2.
- Uterine endometrial (UCEC) has a median of 3.

**Highest TMB (median):** SKCM 15.3, LUSC 7.7, LUAD 6.9 and BLCA 5.9. UCEC has the highest mean TMB (35.6) but a median of only 2.6, because a small group of hypermutated tumors pulls the mean up.

## Correlation with mutation burden

The coefficients below are descriptive. I haven't run a significance test on any of them.

| Level | Measure | Value |
|---|---|---|
| All samples pooled (n=9,975) | Pearson, aneuploidy vs. TMB | −0.05 |
| All samples pooled | Pearson, aneuploidy vs. log10(TMB) | 0.17 |
| All samples pooled | Spearman (approximate, because tied ranks aren't averaged) | about 0.31 |
| Across the 32 cancer types | Pearson of per-type medians | 0.33 |
| Across the 32 cancer types | Pearson of per-type means | 0.13 |
| Across the 32 cancer types | Pearson, mean aneuploidy vs. log10(mean TMB) | 0.35 |

**Within individual cancer types** the correlation is mostly weak, ranging from −0.39 to +0.34:
- **Negative:** UCS (−0.39), COADREAD (−0.36), STAD (−0.28) and UCEC (−0.23).
- **Positive:** DLBC (0.34, n=41), PCPG (0.23), KICH (0.21), LUAD (0.20) and SARC (0.20).
- **Near zero:** most other types, including BRCA, HNSC, KIRC and LGG.

## Interpretation

- Aneuploidy and mutation burden are only loosely related. There is a modest positive trend when you compare cancer types, especially on a rank or log scale. The lung cancers (LUAD, LUSC) and bladder (BLCA) are high on both measures.
- Several cancer types are high on only one measure:
  - TGCT, ACC and KICH are highly aneuploid with low TMB.
  - SKCM has high TMB with only moderate aneuploidy.
  - UCEC and COADREAD have a hypermutated subset with low aneuploidy.
- The negative within-type correlations in UCEC, COADREAD and STAD are consistent with hypermutated tumors having less aneuploidy. This explanation is general background knowledge, not something I tested here. I didn't check MSI status or POLE mutations.
- The raw Pearson values are sensitive to extreme TMB outliers, so I'd rely on the log-scale and rank-based values.
- To get p-values or confidence intervals, run `cor.test(..., method="spearman")` in R or `scipy.stats.spearmanr` in Python on exported per-sample values.

## Explore it in cBioPortal

[Aneuploidy score vs. TMB scatter plot across all 32 TCGA PanCancer Atlas studies](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/plots?id=acc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cblca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cbrca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ccesc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cchol_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ccoadread_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cdlbc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cesca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cgbm_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Chnsc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ckich_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ckirc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ckirp_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Claml_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Clgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Clihc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cluad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Clusc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cmeso_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cov_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cpaad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cpcpg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cprad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Csarc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cskcm_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cstad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ctgct_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cthca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cthym_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cucec_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cucs_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cuvm_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&plots_horz_selection=%7B%22dataType%22%3A%22clinical_attribute%22%2C%22selectedDataSourceOption%22%3A%22TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS%22%2C%22logScale%22%3A%22true%22%7D&plots_vert_selection=%7B%22dataType%22%3A%22clinical_attribute%22%2C%22selectedDataSourceOption%22%3A%22ANEUPLOIDY_SCORE%22%7D)

The portal plot shows TMB on a log scale (x-axis) against aneuploidy score (y-axis). Because the 32 studies are combined, the cohorts overlap in the plot's sample totals and the same patients are not double-counted across studies.

# Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

## Recommended Approach: Use clinical_data_derived

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

```sql
-- Get clinical data for specific attributes
SELECT
    sample_unique_id,
    patient_unique_id,
    attribute_name,
    attribute_value
FROM clinical_data_derived
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    AND attribute_name IN ('CANCER_TYPE', 'SAMPLE_TYPE', 'TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS');
```

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. The shape "altered/not altered × group A/group B" needs Fisher's exact + a defined direction (odds ratio < 1 with significant p). Without that test, the agent presents the table and stops. Descriptive phrasing is also a claim: "largely/mostly mutually exclusive", "rarely co-occur", "tend to co-occur" are forbidden without the test — point to cBioPortal's Mutual Exclusivity tab instead.

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_metabric'
ORDER BY profile_type;

question.question: What fraction of patients were older than five when diagnosed according to the Pediatric Neuroblastoma study from TARGET?

reply.answer:
In the Pediatric Neuroblastoma (TARGET, 2018) study, **125 of 1,076 patients (about 11.6%)** were older than five at diagnosis. All 1,076 patients with a recorded age are in the denominator.

- The other 951 patients (88.4%) were five or younger. That includes 126 patients whose recorded age is 5.
- The study stores age in days as well as whole years. The two measures agree: the oldest "age 5" patient was 1,824 days old, and the youngest "age 6" patient was 1,827 days old. Five years is about 1,826 days, so no patient falls ambiguously on the cutoff.

[View the patients older than five in the study](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=nbl_target_2018_pub#filterJson=%7B%22clinicalDataFilters%22%3A%5B%7B%22attributeId%22%3A%22AGE_IN_DAYS%22%2C%22values%22%3A%5B%7B%22start%22%3A1826.25%7D%5D%7D%5D%7D)

There are other TARGET neuroblastoma datasets. I used the 2018 publication cohort, "Pediatric Neuroblastoma (TARGET, 2018)" (`nbl_target_2018_pub`), because it matches the name you gave. There is also a separate "Neuroblastoma (TARGET GDC, 2025)" study, which I did not query.

# Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

## Recommended Approach: Use clinical_data_derived

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

```sql
-- Get clinical data for specific attributes
SELECT
    sample_unique_id,
    patient_unique_id,
    attribute_name,
    attribute_value
FROM clinical_data_derived
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    AND attribute_name IN ('CANCER_TYPE', 'SAMPLE_TYPE', 'TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS');
```

## Clinical Attribute Discovery

### Use clinical_attribute_meta for Discovering Available Attributes
**Always start here** to see what clinical attributes are available for a specific study:

```sql
-- Discover available clinical attributes for a study
SELECT
    attr_id,
    description,
    patient_attribute,
    cancer_study_id
FROM clinical_attribute_meta
WHERE … (18573 more chars)

question.question: Which KRAS mutations are most common in colorectal cancer?

reply.answer:
**KRAS mutations in colorectal cancer** (TCGA PanCancer Atlas colorectal adenocarcinoma, 534 samples profiled for mutations)

KRAS is mutated in 218 of 534 samples (40.8%). The hotspot changes at codons 12 and 13 dominate. These are the most common protein changes, counted by sample:

| Rank | KRAS mutation | Samples | % of profiled |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | G12D | 58 | 10.9% |
| 2 | G12V | 49 | 9.2% |
| 3 | G13D | 37 | 6.9% |
| 4 | A146T | 16 | 3.0% |
| 5 | G12C | 15 | 2.8% |
| 6 | G12A | 10 | 1.9% |
| 7 | G12S | 8 | 1.5% |
| 8 | Q61H | 4 | 0.7% |
| 8 | K117N | 4 | 0.7% |
| 10 | Q61K | 3 | 0.6% |

Less common changes include G13C, G12R and Q61R (2 samples each).

All of the variants listed are missense mutations. Percentages use samples as the unit. A sample with more than one KRAS mutation is counted under each one, so the rows may not sum exactly to 40.8%.

This is one cohort. Frequencies in other colorectal studies may differ, depending on cohort composition and sequencing approach. Other colorectal studies are available on the portal, including [Colorectal Adenocarcinoma (MSK, 2026)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=crc_msk_2026), [Metastatic Colorectal Cancer (MSK, Cancer Cell 2018)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=crc_msk_2017) and [Colorectal Cancer – ChangKang Project (SYSUCC, 2022)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=crc_sysucc_2022).

[View the KRAS lollipop plot and mutation table in the Mutations tab](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/mutations?cancer_study_list=coadread_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&gene_list=KRAS%3A+MUT&case_set_id=coadread_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018_all)

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.

reply.answer:
I can't give you a median survival time for this cohort from the data I have. Median survival has to come from a Kaplan-Meier estimate that accounts for censoring. A plain median of the follow-up times would be wrong, because patients who were still alive at last follow-up haven't had the event yet.

The cohort is [Pediatric Neuroblastoma (TARGET, 2018)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=nbl_target_2018_pub), which has 1,089 samples. This is the TARGET study with "Pediatric Neuroblastoma" in its name. TARGET also has a separate GDC neuroblastoma study, `nbl_target_gdc`, which I didn't use.

Here is the overall survival (OS) summary, counted by patient:

| | Patients | % |
|---|---|---|
| With OS data | 1,072 | 100% |
| Deceased (event) | 397 | 37% |
| Living (censored) | 675 | 63% |

Follow-up ranges from 1 to 183 months.

Fewer than half of the patients have died, so the Kaplan-Meier median for the whole cohort is likely not reached.

To get the Kaplan-Meier curve and median for the whole cohort, you can use R (`survival::survfit`) or Python (`lifelines.KaplanMeierFitter`). I've also set up a [Kaplan-Meier survival comparison by risk group](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/survival?comparisonId=6b06d8877a1acaed1b1d97b9) in cBioPortal. It compares High Risk (798 samples), Intermediate Risk (121) and Low Risk (168), and shows the per-group curves, medians and log-rank p-value.

You can also [explore the cohort in the Study View](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=nbl_target_2018_pub).

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). 2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. # Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

question.question: In the TCGA glioblastoma study (Cell 2013), how does methylation of the MGMT gene promoter affect the prognosis and treatment response in patients with glioblastoma?
question.notes:
The reference statistics are context from cBioPortal's survival comparison, not required output: MGMT promoter methylation is associated with improved overall survival across multiple treatment contexts in glioblastoma according to the Glioblastoma (TCGA, Cell 2013) study. Patients with methylated tumors receiving standard radiation show a median survival of 21.2 months (95% CI 7.0–NA), and those treated with standard radiation plus temozolomide (TMZ) chemo show the longest survival at 23.5 months (22.2–47.9). Methylated tumors treated with TMZ chemoradiation plus TMZ achieve a median survival of 17.8 months (15.7–21.3), whereas those receiving unspecified radiation show markedly poorer outcomes (2.2 months, 1.4–3.9). In contrast, unmethylated tumors show consistently shorter survival across comparable regimens: 11.6 months (10.3–NA) with standard radiation, 12.7 months (11.7–19.3) with standard radiation plus TMZ, 14.5 months (12.9–15.9) with TMZ chemoradiation plus TMZ, and 2.7 months (1.2–5.4) with unspecified radiation. Across all groups, survival curves for methylated tumors cluster at higher survival times, indicating that MGMT promoter methylation confers both a prognostic advantage and increased benefit from TMZ-containing therapy.
The agent cannot run Kaplan-Meier or log-rank tests. Group comparison links are session-based (`comparisonId` differs on every run): judge a comparison link by the groups and view the rendered page shows, not by matching the reference id or URL.
A correct answer must: compare survival of MGMT-methylated vs unmethylated patients in gbm_tcga_pub2013 (optionally by treatment) and give a working cBioPortal survival comparison link for them, handing off the statistics to cBioPortal.
Must not: invent p-values, hazard ratios or medians, or report a median computed from raw OS_MONTHS values.

reply.answer:
I can't give you a firm answer on prognosis from this cohort. The data are in the study, but the survival comparison needs a Kaplan-Meier (KM) analysis and log-rank test. I can't run those here, so I haven't reported a median survival, hazard ratio or p-value. The comparison page linked below runs them for you.

## MGMT status in the TCGA Glioblastoma study (Cell 2013, 577 samples)

The study records MGMT promoter status as **Methylated** or **Unmethylated**. It is available for 350 of the 577 patients.

| MGMT promoter status | Patients | With survival data | Deaths | Alive at last follow-up |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Methylated | 170 | 169 | 115 | 54 |
| Unmethylated | 180 | 179 | 131 | 48 |
| Not available | 227 | 193 | 171 | 22 |

- Among patients with a status, a somewhat smaller share of the methylated group had died: 115/169 (68%) versus 131/179 (73%). That is a crude proportion that ignores follow-up time, so it doesn't establish a survival difference.
- Follow-up ranges from 0 to about 100 months in the methylated group and 0 to about 128 months in the unmethylated group.
- More than half of each group had died, so I'd expect a KM median to be reachable in both. Compare the two curves rather than the raw counts.

[Open the Kaplan-Meier survival comparison (methylated vs unmethylated)](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/survival?comparisonId=6b06d89023c163a9861d97ba) for the survival curves, log-rank p-value and median survival of each group.

## Treatment response

The study doesn't record treatment response (for example response rate or progression on temozolomide). It has a `THERAPY` field that describes the therapy a patient received. It also has disease-free survival data. The study isn't a trial, so treatment wasn't assigned in a controlled way.

The largest treatment group is **temozolomide (TMZ) chemoradiation plus TMZ chemotherapy**, with 83 methylated and 80 unmethylated patients:

| Group (TMZ chemoradiation + TMZ chemo) | Patients | Deaths | Alive at last follow-up |
|---|---|---|---|
| Methylated | 83 | 47 | 36 |
| Unmethylated | 80 | 52 | 28 |

- Within this group, fewer methylated patients had died (47/83, 57%) than unmethylated patients (52/80, 65%).
- This is an uncontrolled, descriptive count. It doesn't show that methylation predicts benefit from temozolomide.
- Most other treatment subgroups have fewer than 30 patients. They are too small to interpret.
- The study has no untreated comparison group, so whether MGMT status predicts response specifically to temozolomide can't be separated from its general prognostic effect.

To test this properly, restrict the survival comparison to the TMZ-treated patients and run it in cBioPortal. You can also pull the survival times and statuses (`OS_MONTHS`, `OS_STATUS`) into R (`survival::survfit` and `coxph`). A model adjusted for age and treatment is the best way to separate prognosis from treatment effect.

## Other links
- [Study summary for the TCGA Glioblastoma (Cell 2013) cohort](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=gbm_tcga_pub2013)
- [Methylated group (170 samples)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=gbm_tcga_pub2013#filterJson=%7B%22clinicalDataFilters%22%3A%5B%7B%22attributeId%22%3A%22MGMT_STATUS%22%2C%22values%22%3A%5B%7B%22value%22%3A%22METHYLATED%22%7D%5D%7D%5D%7D)

# Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

```sql

SELECT

graded.question: In the TCGA glioblastoma study (Cell 2013), how does methylation of the MGMT gene promoter affect the prognosis and treatment response in patients with glioblastoma?
graded.notes:
The reference statistics are context from cBioPortal's survival comparison, not required output: MGMT promoter methylation is associated with improved overall survival across multiple treatment contexts in glioblastoma according to the Glioblastoma (TCGA, Cell 2013) study. Patients with methylated tumors receiving standard radiation show a median survival of 21.2 months (95% CI 7.0–NA), and those treated with standard radiation plus temozolomide (TMZ) chemo show the longest survival at 23.5 months (22.2–47.9). Methylated tumors treated with TMZ chemoradiation plus TMZ achieve a median survival of 17.8 months (15.7–21.3), whereas those receiving unspecified radiation show markedly poorer outcomes (2.2 months, 1.4–3.9). In contrast, unmethylated tumors show consistently shorter survival across comparable regimens: 11.6 months (10.3–NA) with standard radiation, 12.7 months (11.7–19.3) with standard radiation plus TMZ, 14.5 months (12.9–15.9) with TMZ chemoradiation plus TMZ, and 2.7 months (1.2–5.4) with unspecified radiation. Across all groups, survival curves for methylated tumors cluster at higher survival times, indicating that MGMT promoter methylation confers both a prognostic advantage and increased benefit from TMZ-containing therapy.
The agent cannot run Kaplan-Meier or log-rank tests. Group comparison links are session-based (`comparisonId` differs on every run): judge a comparison link by the groups and view the rendered page shows, not by matching the reference id or URL.
A correct answer must: compare survival of MGMT-methylated vs unmethylated patients in gbm_tcga_pub2013 (optionally by treatment) and give a working cBioPortal survival comparison link for them, handing off the statistics to cBioPortal.
Must not: invent p-values, hazard ratios or medians, or report a median computed from raw OS_MONTHS values.

question.question: In the “Pan-cancer analysis of whole genomes” study what is the survival difference and the corresponding statistical significance between patients with mutations in both TP53 and KRAS versus patients with only a KRAS mutation?
question.expected_answer: This comparison is not meaningful in the Pan-cancer analysis of whole genomes study: only 282 patients have overall survival data, and just 1 of them has both TP53 and KRAS mutations and 3 have only a KRAS mutation, so no reliable median survival or p-value can be computed.
question.notes: A correct answer must say there are too few patients with survival data and both mutations to compare; must not invent a median or p-value.

reply.answer:
**I can't give you a survival difference or a p-value for this comparison, because the study has almost no usable survival data for these patients.**

**Cohort:** Pan-cancer analysis of whole genomes (ICGC/TCGA, Nature 2020), study ID `pancan_pcawg_2020`. Counts are by patient.

| Group | Patients | With a recorded survival time and status | Deaths among those | Alive/censored among those |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| KRAS and TP53 both mutated | 187 | **1** | 0 | 1 (33.5 months) |
| KRAS mutated, TP53 not mutated | 85 | **3** | 0 | 3 (0 to 29.6 months) |

- **Survival times are mostly missing.** Only about 280 of the 2,658 patients in the study have a recorded survival time. For these KRAS-mutant patients that leaves 4 in total, and none of them died.
- **Status without a time can't be used.** Many other patients have a vital status (deceased or living) but no time. They can't go into a Kaplan-Meier curve or a log-rank test.
- **No test can be run.** A Kaplan-Meier comparison and log-rank test need both a time and a status for each patient. With 1 patient in one group, 3 in the other and no deaths, there's nothing to compare. I haven't computed a p-value, hazard ratio or median survival, and any figure for them would be invented.
- **Group sizes differ slightly.** The portal counts 187 and 86 samples, against 187 and 85 patients above. This is probably one patient with two samples.

You can open the same comparison in the portal's Survival tab. It will show how few patients have survival data, and it computes the log-rank test itself:

- [KRAS + TP53 mutated vs KRAS mutated only: Survival comparison](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/survival?comparisonId=6b06d89e214c562d5a916ac1)
- [Study overview](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=pancan_pcawg_2020)

If you want a survival answer for KRAS/TP53 co-mutation, a study with complete follow-up would work better. TCGA PanCancer Atlas cohorts such as pancreatic, lung adenocarcinoma or colorectal are options, and I can set up the same comparison there.

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_metabric'
ORDER BY profile_type;

question.question: For patients with the EML4-ALK fusion gene in lung cancer how do the different fusion variants affect their long-term quality of life and risk of developing a secondary cancer?
question.expected_answer: This question cannot be answered with the cBioPortal databse
question.notes: Out of scope. A correct answer must say cBioPortal can't answer this; must not invent an answer.

reply.answer:
I'll check what the database holds on EML4-ALK fusion variants, quality of life, and second cancers.The database has no quality-of-life data and no second-cancer data for lung cohorts. I'll pull the study metadata so I can link you to the fusion data that does exist.**The cBioPortal data can't answer this question.** It has no quality-of-life data and no second-cancer data for EML4-ALK lung cancer patients, so I can't link variants to either outcome.

## What the data does and doesn't contain

**Quality of life**
- I found no quality-of-life or patient-reported outcome measures, such as FACT or EORTC scores, in any study.
- The ALK-fusion lung cohort (alk_msk_2026) has overall survival (`OS_MONTHS`, `OS_STATUS`), stage, smoking prediction and metastatic site. None of these measures quality of life.

**Second primary cancers**
- Only two studies have a second-cancer attribute: a cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma study (`cscc_dfarber_2015`) and a breast cancer study (`brca_aurora_2023`).
- Neither is a lung or ALK cohort. I found no second-cancer field in any lung or ALK-fusion cohort.

**Fusion variants**
- Variant-level detail is patchy. In most studies, the EML4-ALK calls are recorded only as "in frame" or "mid-exon", with no exon numbers.
- In the ALK-fusion cohort (alk_msk_2026) and MSK-MET (`msk_met_2021`), many calls carry free-text breakpoint descriptions. For example, ALK breakpoints fall before exon 20, and EML4 breakpoints fall near exons 6 and 13, among others.
- Exon-level annotation is structured only in `lung_nci_2022` (13 fusions). Because that is so small, I did not group patients by variant.
- I did not compare survival across variants.

## Cohorts with EML4-ALK fusion calls

Patient counts per study. These cohorts overlap, so don't add them together, and some include non-lung tumors.

| Study | Patients with EML4-ALK |
|---|---|
| MSK-CHORD 2024 | 203 |
| MSK-IMPACT 50k | 181 |
| MSK-MET 2021 | 147 |
| OrigiMed pan-cancer 2020 | 111 |
| NSCLC, MSK 2026 (ALK TKI resistance cohort) | 53 |

## Where to look in cBioPortal

- [ALK/EML4 structural variant table, NSCLC MSK 2026](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/structuralVariants?cancer_study_list=alk_msk_2026&gene_list=ALK%3A+FUSION%0AEML4%3A+FUSION&case_set_id=alk_msk_2026_all) shows the individual fusion calls with their breakpoints.
- [NSCLC MSK 2026 study overview](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=alk_msk_2026) and [MSK-CHORD 2024](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=msk_chord_2024) both support group comparisons, including survival.

Overall survival is the only outcome available to compare, and it isn't a quality-of-life or second-cancer measure. Any survival comparison between variants needs a Kaplan-Meier analysis, which I haven't run.

For quality of life and second cancers, you would need a prospective cohort or registry, or the primary literature. That is outside what cBioPortal holds. This is for research purposes only, and I can't offer clinical advice or prognosis.

This guide highlights frequent mistakes when analyzing cBioPortal data and provides solutions to avoid them.

### 1. 🚨 CRITICAL MUTATION FREQUENCY ERRORS

```sql

# Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)

# Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

## Recommended Approach: Use clinical_data_derived

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

```sql
-- Get clinical data for specific attributes
SELECT
    sample_unique_id,
    patient_unique_id,
    attribute_name,
    attribute_value
FROM clinical_data_derived
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    AND attribute_name IN ('CANCER_TYPE', 'SAMPLE_TYPE', 'TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS');
```

## Clinical Attribute Discovery

### Use clinical_attribute_meta for Discovering Available Attributes
**Always start here** to see what clinical attributes are available for a specific study:

SELECT

question.question: Are there studies that were not processed using polyA enrichment in order to explore lncRNA-related questions?
question.expected_answer: Library preparation protocols are not contained in the database and should be consulted in the publications underlying the studies.
question.notes: Out of scope. A correct answer must say cBioPortal can't answer this; must not invent an answer.

reply.answer:
**Short answer:** cBioPortal doesn't record library prep (polyA selection, ribo-depletion, total RNA) as a searchable field. I found no study whose description says "ribo-depleted", "total RNA" or "rRNA-depleted". The only evidence is how some studies label their expression profiles, so treat the list below as leads to check in the original publications.

**Studies that label their RNA-seq as capture-based, so not polyA**

| Study | What the profile label says |
|---|---|
| [Metastatic Prostate Adenocarcinoma (SU2C/PCF, PNAS 2019)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=prad_su2c_2019) | Has two separate sets of expression profiles, one "FPKM capture" and one "FPKM polyA". This is the only study I found that includes both prep types. |
| [Prostate cancer (Eur Urol 2017)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=prad_eururol_2017) | "mRNA expression from capture (RNA Seq FPKM)" |
| [Lung adenocarcinoma (CAS 2020)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=luad_cas_2020) | "mRNA expression from capture (RNA Seq FPKM)" |
| [GBM CPTAC 2021](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=gbm_cptac_2021) | "FPKM capture" |
| [PCAWG pan-cancer 2020](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=pancan_pcawg_2020) | Profile ID contains "fpkm_capture" |

For the SU2C 2019 study, you can analyze the capture and polyA profiles side by side.

**Explicitly polyA:** the SU2C/PCF [2015](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=prad_su2c_2015) and [2019](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=prad_su2c_2019) prostate studies. These are the ones to avoid if you want non-polyA data, or to use as the polyA comparison.

**Caveat on the GDC-harmonized studies:** many of these studies (the TCGA, CPTAC and TARGET "_gdc" ones, such as [brca_tcga_gdc](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=brca_tcga_gdc)) carry the same "from capture" wording. It looks like a generic template label rather than a true statement about library prep. I wouldn't rely on it.

**lncRNA coverage**
- The portal's gene list includes about 6,400 ncRNA entries. Well-known lncRNAs such as MALAT1, NEAT1, HOTAIR, H19, XIST and PCA3 have expression values in the studies I checked.
- These were the SU2C 2015 and 2019 studies, Eur Urol 2017, GBM CPTAC 2021, PCAWG, brca_tcga_gdc and St. Jude pediatric AML 2024. LUAD CAS 2020 had every one of them except MALAT1 and PCA3, so its lncRNA coverage is more limited.
- [CCLE 2025](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=ccle_broad_2025) describes its expression data as protein-coding genes only, so it isn't suitable for lncRNA work.
- The [St. Jude pediatric AML 2024 study](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=aml_stjude_2024) has lncRNA expression, but its prep method isn't stated.

**Recommendation:** for a firm answer on library prep, check each study's publication or its GDC/dbGaP methods, especially for the capture-labeled studies. Once you've chosen a study, I can pull lncRNA expression for it.

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_metabric'
ORDER BY profile_type;
```

Common values across the public portal:

| Family | Profile types |

| mRNA expression | `rna_seq_v2_mrna`, `rna_seq_v2_mrna_median_Zscores`, `rna_seq_v2_mrna_median_all_sample_Zscores` (TCGA Pan … (6431 more chars)

# cBioPortal FAQ Guide

Curated answers to frequently asked general questions about cBioPortal. Source: [cBioPortal FAQ](https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/).

## What is cBioPortal?

cBioPortal for Cancer Genomics is an open-access, open-source resource for interactive exploration of multidimensional cancer genomics data sets. It was originally developed at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) and is now maintained by a multi-institutional team.

## History

- **2008**: cBioPortal first became available online.
- **2012**: First major publication — Cerami et al., *Cancer Discovery*.
- **2013**: Second major publication — Gao et al., *Science Signaling*.
- **2023**: Third major publication — de Bruijn et al., *Cancer Research*.

## How to Cite cBioPortal

When using cBioPortal in publications, cite these three papers:

1. Cerami et al. "The cBio Cancer Genomics Portal: An Open Platform for Exploring Multidimensional Cancer Genomics Data." *Cancer Discovery* 2, 401–404 (2012). doi:10.1158/2159-8290.CD-12-0095
2. Gao et al. "Integrative Analysis of Complex Cancer Genomics and Clinical Profiles Using the cBioPortal." *Science Signaling* 6, pl1 (2013). doi:10.1126/scisignal.2004088
3. de Bruijn et al. "Analysis and Visualization of Longitudinal Genomic and Clinical Data from the AACR Project GENIE Biopharma Collaborative in cBioPortal." *Cancer Research* 83, 3861–3867 (2023). doi:10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-23-0816

question.question: In the Pediatric Neuroblastoma study from TARGET what is the survival difference and the corresponding statistical significance between patients who were older than four when diagnosed and the younger ones?
question.expected_answer: Older patients (>4) had significantly worse overall survival compared to younger patients (≤4) with a higher hazard of death (HR = 1.47; 95% CI 1.17–1.86; log-rank p = 3.37×10⁻⁴). Their median overall survival was 79.0 months (95% CI 53–122) whereas median survival was not reached in the ≤4 group.
question.notes:
The reference statistics are context from cBioPortal's survival comparison, not required output (log-rank p=3.37e-4; KM median 79.0 months for >4 years, not reached for <=4 years). The agent cannot run Kaplan-Meier or log-rank tests. Group comparison links are session-based (`comparisonId` differs on every run): judge a comparison link by the groups and view the rendered page shows, not by matching the reference id or URL.
A correct answer must: define the two groups by age at diagnosis (>4 vs <=4 years) in nbl_target_2018_pub and give a working cBioPortal survival comparison link for them, handing off the statistics to cBioPortal.
Must not: invent p-values, hazard ratios or medians, or report a median computed from raw OS_MONTHS values.

reply.answer:
I can't give you a log-rank p-value or a survival-difference estimate. The database I query can't run Kaplan-Meier or log-rank tests, so I haven't made up a number. The Survival tab link below runs the test for you.

**Cohort:** [Pediatric Neuroblastoma (TARGET, 2018)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=nbl_target_2018_pub). I split patients by age at diagnosis, using age in days: older than 4 years is more than 1,461 days.

**Overall survival summary (patients with survival data):**

| Group | Patients | Deaths | Censored (alive at last follow-up) | Follow-up range (months) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Older than 4 years | 250 | 121 (48%) | 129 | 1–183 |
| 4 years or younger | 822 | 276 (34%) | 546 | 1–183 |

- **Event rates:** The older group had a higher share of deaths, but this is not a survival comparison. Follow-up times differ between patients and many are censored, so the proportions can mislead.
- **Median survival:** Fewer than half of the 4-years-or-younger group died, so the Kaplan-Meier median is probably not reached in that group.

**Statistical significance:**
- **Test:** The right test is Kaplan-Meier with a log-rank test. A hazard ratio would need Cox regression.
- **Survival tab:** [Open the Overall Survival comparison](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/survival?comparisonId=6b06d8bdd43336d887916ac2). It shows the Kaplan-Meier curves, median survival and the log-rank p-value for the two groups. The page lists 253 vs 836 samples. That is slightly more than the patient counts above because some patients have more than one sample.
- **R or Python:** You can also run `survival::survfit` and `survdiff` in R, or `lifelines` in Python, on the OS_MONTHS and OS_STATUS fields.

**Assumptions:**
- I took "older than four" as strictly more than 4 years (more than 1,461 days).
- I used overall survival. If you meant event-free survival, tell me and I can set that up.

[Study overview](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=nbl_target_2018_pub)

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. The shape "altered/not altered × group A/group B" needs Fisher's exact + a defined direction (odds ratio < 1 with significant p). Without that test, the agent presents the table and stops. Descriptive phrasing is also a claim: "largely/mostly mutually exclusive", "rarely co-occur", "tend to co-occur" are forbidden without the test — point to cBioPortal's Mutual Exclusivity tab instead.
3. **Never report a "median" that came from `AVG(...)` or any non-median aggregate.** "Median" and "mean" are differen … (11484 more chars)

# Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

## Recommended Approach: Use clinical_data_derived

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

```sql
-- Get clinical data for specific attributes
SELECT
    sample_unique_id,
    patient_unique_id,
    attribute_name,
    attribute_value
FROM clinical_data_derived
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    AND attribute_name IN ('CANCER_TYPE', 'SAMPLE_TYPE', 'TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS');
```

## Clinical Attribute Discovery

### Use clinical_attribute_meta for Discovering Available Attributes
**Always start here** to see what clinical attributes are available for a specific study:

```sql
-- Discover available clinical attributes for a study
SELECT
    attr_id,
    description,
    patient_attribute,
    cancer_study_id
FROM clinical_attribute_meta

question.question: In the TCGA PanCancer Atlas breast cancer study, what is the correlation coefficient between EGFR expression levels and PIK3CA mutation status considering only patients who also have a homozygous deletion of PTEN?

reply.answer:
Among the 55 patients in the TCGA PanCancer Atlas breast study (Breast Invasive Carcinoma) with a homozygous (deep) PTEN deletion, the Spearman correlation between EGFR mRNA expression and PIK3CA mutation status is about **0.27**.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Samples with PTEN deep deletion and EGFR expression data | 55 |
| Samples with a PIK3CA mutation | 6 |
| Samples with wild-type PIK3CA | 49 |
| Spearman correlation (EGFR mRNA vs. PIK3CA mutated = 1, wild-type = 0) | 0.27 |
| Point-biserial (Pearson) correlation, raw RSEM values | −0.08 |
| Point-biserial (Pearson) correlation, log2(RSEM+1) values | −0.17 |

- **Different methods, different signs:** The Spearman result is positive, while both Pearson results are slightly negative. All of them are weak, and the sign depends on the method.
- **Small mutant group:** With only 6 mutated samples, none of these estimates is stable. I haven't computed a p-value or confidence interval, so I can't say whether any of them differs from zero.
- **Binary variable:** PIK3CA status is mutated or wild-type, so a correlation coefficient is a rough summary. Comparing EGFR expression between the two groups is a more natural test. A t-test on log2 expression is the usual choice.
- **How I counted:**
  - Each unit is a sample.
  - PTEN deletion means a GISTIC value of −2.
  - PIK3CA mutated means any called mutation within the panel coverage.
  - EGFR expression is the non-z-scored RSEM mRNA value.

[Open the EGFR expression by PIK3CA mutation plot, restricted to the 55 PTEN-deleted samples](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/plots?session_id=6b06d8cd1ae8a80c27916ac3). You can also [explore the PTEN-deleted cohort in the Study View](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018#filterJson=%7B%22genomicDataFilters%22%3A%5B%7B%22hugoGeneSymbol%22%3A%22PTEN%22%2C%22profileType%22%3A%22gistic%22%2C%22values%22%3A%5B%7B%22value%22%3A%22-2%22%7D%5D%7D%5D%7D).

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_metabric'
ORDER BY profile_type;
```

Common values across the public portal:

| Family | Profile types |

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. The shape "altered/not altered × group A/group B" needs Fisher's exact + a defined direction (odds ratio < 1 with significant p). Without that test, the agent presents the table and stops. {"query": "WITH del AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT sample_unique_id FROM genomic_event_derived
  WHERE cancer_study_identifier='brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018' AND hugo_gene_symbol='PTEN' AND variant_type='cna' AND cna_alteration=-2
),
mut AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT sample_unique_id FROM genomic_event_derived
  WHERE cancer_study_identifier='brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018' AND hugo_gene_symbol='PIK3CA' AND variant_type='mutation' AND mutation_status!='UNCALLED' AND off_panel=0
),
sq AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT sample_unique_id FROM genetic_alteration_derived
  WHERE cancer_study_identifier='brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018' AND profile_type='gistic' AND hugo_gene_symbol='PTEN' AND alteration_value='-2'
),
expr AS (
  SELECT sample_unique_id, toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) AS v FROM genetic_alteration_derived
  WHERE cancer_study_identifier='brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018' AND profile_type='rna_seq_v2_mrna' AND hugo_gene_symbol='EGFR'
    AND alteration_value NOT IN ('','NA') AND toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT (SELECT count() FROM del) AS n_del_event, (SELECT count() FROM sq) AS n_del_gistic,
 count() AS n, sum(m) AS n_mut, rankCorr(v, m) AS spearman, corr(v, m) AS pearson_pb, corr(log2(v+1), m) AS pearson_log
FROM (SELECT e.sample_unique_id, e.v AS v, if(e.sample_unique_id IN (SELECT sample_unique_id FROM mut),1,0) AS m
      FROM expr e WHERE e.sample_unique_id IN (SELECT sample_unique_id FROM del))"}

question.question: In the TCGA PanCancer Atlas breast cancer study, what is the average tumor mutational burden of patients who have at least two of the five most frequently mutated genes and how does this compare to the average TMB of all patients?
question.expected_answer: Top 5 mutated genes: TP53, PIK3CA, TTN, CDH1, GATA3. 296 patients have ≥2 of them; their mean TMB is 5.5 mut/Mb (median 2.0) vs 2.7 (median 1.3) for all 1,066 patients (TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS).
question.notes: Means are skewed by hypermutated tumors (TTN is a long gene); mentioning medians or this caveat is good.

reply.answer:
Patients with at least two of the five most frequently mutated genes have a mean TMB of about 5.5 mutations/Mb. That is roughly double the cohort-wide mean of 2.7 mutations/Mb.

**Cohort:** Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas). It has 1,084 patients, each with one sample. 1,066 of them are profiled for mutations and have a TMB value, and the analysis uses those.

**Five most frequently mutated genes** (share of the 1,066 profiled patients with a mutation in the gene):
| Gene | Patients mutated | % |
|---|---|---|
| PIK3CA | 347 | 32.6% |
| TP53 | 347 | 32.6% |
| TTN | 187 | 17.5% |
| CDH1 | 130 | 12.2% |
| GATA3 | 127 | 11.9% |

**TMB comparison** (TMB = nonsynonymous mutations per Mb):
| Group | Patients | Mean TMB | Median TMB |
|---|---|---|---|
| ≥2 of the top 5 genes mutated | 296 (27.8%) | **5.53** | 2.03 |
| Fewer than 2 of the top 5 | 770 | 1.66 | 1.17 |
| **All patients** | 1,066 | **2.73** | 1.30 |

- The mean for the ≥2-gene group is about 2.0× the all-patient mean. It is about 3.3× the mean of the remaining patients.
- The medians are much closer together (2.03 vs 1.30). A small number of hypermutated tumors pull the group mean up, so the difference in means overstates the typical gap.
- Part of the difference is built in. TTN is a very large gene that is often mutated by chance, and tumors with more mutations are more likely to carry mutations in several of these genes.
- I haven't run a significance test. The difference is descriptive only.

I counted a patient if they had at least one non-"uncalled" mutation in each qualifying gene. Eighteen patients have no TMB value and are excluded.

**Explore in cBioPortal:**
- [OncoPrint of the five genes with a TMB track](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/oncoprint?cancer_study_list=brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&gene_list=PIK3CA%3A+MUT%0ATP53%3A+MUT%0ATTN%3A+MUT%0ACDH1%3A+MUT%0AGATA3%3A+MUT&case_set_id=brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018_all&clinicallist=TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS). It shows each tumor's mutations in these genes next to its TMB.
- [Study overview](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018)

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.
- **For "across cancer types" questions**, jump to the [Cross-Cancer-Type Mutation Frequency](#cross-cancer-type-mutation-frequency) section below — there is one correct recipe and several common wrong ones.

## Counting Unit: Samples vs Patients

Before answering any mutation count or frequency question, decide whether the unit is samples or patients and state that choice in the answer.

| User wording | Counting unit |

# Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

## Recommended Approach: Use clinical_data_derived

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

```sql
-- Get clinical data for specific attributes
SELECT
    sample_unique_id,
    patient_unique_id,
    attribute_name,
    attribute_value
FROM clinical_data_derived
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    AND attribute_name IN ('CANCER_TYPE', 'SAMPLE_TYPE', 'TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS');
```

================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

## Overview

question.question: In TCGA PanCancer Atlas, which recurrent hotspot mutations occur almost exclusively in one cancer type?
question.expected_answer: Among missense variants with at least 10 carriers across the TCGA PanCancer Atlas studies (by CANCER_TYPE), known driver hotspots that are ≥90% one cancer type include: GTF2I L424H in thymic epithelial tumors (59/61), IDH1 R132H in glioma (358/388, 92%), BRAF V600K in melanoma (35/35), EGFR L858R in non-small cell lung cancer (23/23), GNA11 Q209L and GNAQ Q209L/P in ocular melanoma, PTEN R130G, FGFR2 S252W and PPP2R1A P179R in endometrial cancer, and DNMT3A R882H, IDH2 R140Q and FLT3 D835Y in leukemia. Many other 100%-specific variants are UV-signature passengers in melanoma (e.g. olfactory receptor genes).
question.notes:
No cBioPortal page shows this, so a link is not expected.
A correct answer must: use the TCGA PanCancer Atlas studies (pan_cancer_tcga) grouped by CANCER_TYPE, state its specificity rule (e.g. a minimum carrier count and share of carriers in one cancer type), and name several of the driver hotspots in the reference with counts from the data.
Must not: present melanoma UV passenger variants as cancer-type-specific drivers without saying so, invent counts, or cite hotspots from cancer types that aren't in TCGA (e.g. KIT/PDGFRA in GIST) as TCGA results.

reply.answer:
In TCGA PanCancer Atlas, 10 recurrent missense variants (at least 15 mutated samples pan-cancer) fall almost entirely in one cancer type. Two are fully exclusive: BRAF V600K (melanoma) and EGFR L858R (lung adenocarcinoma).

I counted mutated samples across all 32 PanCancer Atlas studies and kept variants where at least 85% of carriers sit in one study. Each study is one cancer type, so LGG and GBM count separately. I excluded off-panel and uncalled mutations, and counts are samples, not patients.

| Variant | Total mutated samples | Main cancer type | Samples there | Share in that type | Other types (samples) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| IDH1 R132H | 388 | Lower-grade glioma | 358 | 92.3% | GBM 22, AML 5, bladder 1 |
| GTF2I L424H | 61 | Thymoma | 59 | 96.7% | LGG 1, PCPG 1 |
| PTEN R130G | 43 | Endometrial (UCEC) | 41 | 95.3% | GBM 1, UCS 1 |
| GNA11 Q209L | 37 | Uveal melanoma | 34 | 91.9% | Skin melanoma 3 |
| BRAF V600K | 35 | Skin melanoma | 35 | 100% | None |
| GNAQ Q209P | 30 | Uveal melanoma | 27 | 90.0% | Skin melanoma 3 |
| FGFR2 S252W | 26 | Endometrial (UCEC) | 24 | 92.3% | Ovarian 1, UCS 1 |
| EGFR L858R | 23 | Lung adenocarcinoma | 23 | 100% | None |
| DNMT3A R882H | 22 | AML | 21 | 95.5% | Breast 1 |
| IDH2 R140Q | 18 | AML | 17 | 94.4% | Head and neck 1 |

- **Glioma:** IDH1 R132H also appears in GBM (22 samples). That is 6% of its carriers, so it is not strictly exclusive.
- **Melanoma:** GNA11 and GNAQ hotspots are concentrated in uveal melanoma, with a few cases in skin melanoma.
- **Skin melanoma:** At a looser threshold of 10 or more samples, many more variants appear that are exclusive to skin melanoma (for example PPP6C R264C, 11 of 11 samples). I left them out because melanoma's very high mutation burden produces many recurrent-looking variants.
- **BRAF V600E:** It is not on the list because it occurs in several cancer types.

The database doesn't annotate these as hotspots or drivers. "Recurrent" here only means a variant seen in at least 15 samples. For driver or hotspot filtering, use the `MUT_DRIVER` OQL modifier in the portal, which applies OncoKB and hotspot annotations.

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`

question.question: Which patients have a TP53 G199V mutation? Which are somatic vs germline?
question.expected_answer: TP53 G199V appears in 66 distinct patient IDs (180 patient entries across 67 studies; many MSK patients appear in several overlapping studies). Calls are somatic (156 records) or have no status (38); only one is labeled germline: TCGA-A2-A0SX in brca_tcga_pub.
question.notes: A correct answer must deduplicate or warn about patients shared across overlapping studies and must identify the single germline call; listing all patients is not required.

reply.answer:
TP53 G199V (a missense mutation) is recorded in 66 distinct patient IDs across about 90 studies. Exactly one patient has a germline call: TCGA-A2-A0SX, a breast cancer patient in the TCGA Nature 2012 study. That call conflicts with other TCGA releases of the same case. Most of the other patients are labeled somatic, and 17 have no somatic/germline label.

Many studies share patients, for example the MSK-IMPACT, MSK-CHORD and MSK-MET cohorts and the several TCGA releases. The 66 are distinct patient IDs, not independent cases.

## Germline (1 patient)
- **TCGA-A2-A0SX** is germline only in [Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA, Nature 2012)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=brca_tcga_pub).
- The same variant in the same patient is labeled "Somatic" in `brca_tcga` and `brca_tcga_gdc`. It is "." in the PanCancer Atlas and "NA" in the 2015 release.
- The germline call comes from one study, and the other TCGA releases of this case disagree with it. Check the source data before treating it as a confirmed germline variant.
- [Open TP53 G199V in the Nature 2012 study (Mutations tab)](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/mutations?cancer_study_list=brca_tcga_pub&gene_list=TP53%3A+MUT+%3D+G199V&case_set_id=brca_tcga_pub_all)

## Somatic (48 patients, no germline label anywhere)
- **TCGA and CPTAC (9):** TCGA-06-0152, TCGA-AD-6901, TCGA-C8-A27A, TCGA-EJ-8472, TCGA-XF-A9ST, C3L-03976, C3N-02529, C3N-02944 (some releases label these cases "." or "NA").
- **MSK sarcoma (2):** sarcoma_msk_2022-3688, sarcoma_msk_2022-6793.

Overview
--------
cBioPortal stores both somatic AND germline variant data. Many cBioPortal features work identically for both variant types. This guide explains how to query germline variants and what to be aware of.

How Germline Data is Stored
---------------------------

### mutation_status is free text — always compare case-insensitively
Each study loads its own spelling. Germline calls appear as `'Germline'`, `'GERMLINE'` and `'germline'`; somatic calls as `'Somatic'`, `'SOMATIC'` and `'somatic'`; unannotated mutations as `'NA'`, `'.'`, `'Unknown'`, `'UNKNOWN'`, `'__UNKNOWN__'` and others. # Genomic differences between lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) in the Pan-Lung Cancer TCGA study

**Cohort:** [Pan-Lung Cancer (TCGA, Nat Genet 2016)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=nsclc_tcga_broad_2016). It has 660 LUAD and 484 LUSC patients, all with whole-exome sequencing. Percentages below are patients altered ÷ patients in each subtype. Copy-number calls are GISTIC high-level amplifications (AMP) and deep deletions (HOMDEL).

I did not run any statistical tests. The percentages are descriptive. The comparison link at the end runs the formal enrichment tests.

## Somatic mutations

| Gene | LUAD | LUSC | Higher in |
|---|---|---|---|
| **KRAS** | 214 (32.4%) | 8 (1.7%) | LUAD |
| **EGFR** | 104 (15.8%) | 13 (2.7%) | LUAD |
| **STK11** | 104 (15.8%) | 7 (1.4%) | LUAD |
| **BRAF** | 54 (8.2%) | 16 (3.3%) | LUAD |
| **SMARCA4** | 61 (9.2%) | 18 (3.7%) | LUAD |
| **RBM10** | 41 (6.2%) | 6 (1.2%) | LUAD |
| **MET** | 28 (4.2%) | 6 (1.2%) | LUAD |
| **U2AF1** | 17 (2.6%) | 0 | LUAD |
| **TP53** | 357 (54.1%) | 418 (86.4%) | LUSC |
| **KMT2D** | 49 (7.4%) | 114 (23.6%) | LUSC |
| **NFE2L2** | 14 (2.1%) | 70 (14.5%) | LUSC |
| **CDKN2A** | 27 (4.1%) | 75 (15.5%) | LUSC |
| **PTEN** | 11 (1.7%) | 56 (11.6%) | LUSC |
| **PIK3CA** | 39 (5.9%) | 55 (11.4%) | LUSC |
| **NOTCH1** | 31 (4.7%) | 40 (8.3%) | LUSC |

- **LUAD** is enriched for the RTK/RAS/MAPK pathway genes (KRAS, EGFR, BRAF, MET) and for STK11, SMARCA4, RBM10 and U2AF1.
- **LUSC** is enriched for TP53, the oxidative-stress gene NFE2L2, the tumor suppressors CDKN2A and PTEN, the chromatin gene KMT2D, and PIK3CA and NOTCH1.
- KEAP1 and NF1 mutations are present in both subtypes: KEAP1 in 16.7% of LUAD and 10.7% of LUSC, and NF1 in 11.5% and 10.5%.

## Copy-number alterations

| Gene (locus) | LUAD | LUSC | Higher in |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SOX2** (3q26.33) AMP | 15 (2.3%) | 205 (42.4%) | LUSC |
| **PIK3CA** AMP | 14 (2.1%) | 194 (40.1%) | LUSC |
| **TP63** AMP | 13 (2.0%) | 163 (33.7%) | LUSC |
| **FGFR1** AMP | 19 (2.9%) | 83 (17.1%) | LUSC |
| **CCND1** AMP | 26 (3.9%) | 63 (13.0%) | LUSC |
| **PTEN** HOMDEL | 5 (0.8%) | 31 (6.4%) | LUSC |
| **CDKN2A** HOMDEL | 112 (17.0%) | 129 (26.7%) | LUSC |
| **NKX2-1** AMP | 79 (12.0%) | 13 (2.7%) | LUAD |
| **MDM2** AMP | 36 (5.5%) | 10 (2.1%) | LUAD |

- The 3q26–q28 amplicon (SOX2, PIK3CA, TP63) is the largest CNA difference, and it is typical of LUSC.
- NKX2-1 amplification is more frequent in LUAD.
- Amplification of MYC, TERT, EGFR and ERBB2 is similar in the two subtypes.

## Global genomic features
These are medians, and I did not test the differences.

| Feature | LUAD | LUSC |
|---|---|---|
| Fraction of genome altered | 0.24 | 0.39 |
| Non-synonymous TMB (mut/Mb) | 6.27 | 7.07 |

LUSC has more genome-wide copy-number change. Mutation burden is broadly similar, and LUAD has the wider spread (mean 270 vs 256 mutations; median 188 vs 212).

## Caveats
- Frequent mutation does not mean a gene is a driver. I did not use driver annotation here.
- Structural variants are sparse in this dataset, so I can't compare fusions. ROS1 appeared once, in LUAD.
- The genes in the tables were chosen from the largest mutation differences plus a set of well-known lung cancer genes. The tables are not exhaustive.

## Explore and test in cBioPortal
- [Group comparison: LUAD vs LUSC alteration enrichment](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/alterations?comparisonId=6b06d8fadbee5e2826916ac4). This gives p-values and q-values for mutations and CNAs across the full gene set.
- [OncoPrint of KRAS, EGFR, STK11, TP53, SOX2, PIK3CA, NFE2L2, CDKN2A and PTEN, with a histology track](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/oncoprint?cancer_study_list=nsclc_tcga_broad_2016&gene_list=KRAS%0AEGFR%0ASTK11%0ATP53%0ASOX2%0APIK3CA%0ANFE2L2%0ACDKN2A%0APTEN&case_set_id=nsclc_tcga_broad_2016_all&clinicallist=CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED)
- [Study overview](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=nsclc_tcga_broad_2016)
