reply.answer:
These are median mRNA expression values in **Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas)**. The data are RSEM values from RNA-seq (v2) for 177 samples with expression data.

| Gene | Median (RSEM) | Median (log2(RSEM+1)) | Q1–Q3 (RSEM) |
|---|---|---|---|
| MUC1 | 14,799 | 13.85 | 7,581 – 26,642 |
| CEACAM5 | 10,050 | 13.30 | 1,115 – 32,625 |
| ITGB6 | 3,740 | 11.87 | 2,365 – 6,166 |
| TPBG | 857 | 9.74 | 665 – 1,036 |
| MUC2 | 6.5 | 2.91 | 1.4 – 65 |

- **Expression range:** MUC1 has the highest median expression and MUC2 is very low.
- **CEACAM5:** Its interquartile range is wide (about 1,100 to 32,600), so expression varies a lot between tumors.
- **MUC2:** Its Q3 (65) is about ten times its median, which suggests a minority of tumors express it.
- **Cohort choice:** I used the TCGA PanCancer Atlas cohort because it is the standard TCGA pancreatic adenocarcinoma dataset. Other pancreatic studies, such as CPTAC (`paad_cptac_2021`) or QCMG (`paad_qcmg_uq_2016`), use different assays and normalization. Their raw values aren't directly comparable to these.
- **Z-scores:** I didn't use z-scores because they are relative to this cohort. They can't be compared across cohorts.

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_metabric'
ORDER BY profile_type;
```

reply.answer:
Eleven pediatric studies in the portal were published in the last five years (since late 2021). Seven are peer-reviewed papers or publication-linked cohorts, and four are 2025 TARGET GDC data releases that aren't tied to a paper. I treated a study as pediatric if its title or description says pediatric or childhood, or if it comes from the TARGET program. I took the publication year from the study title and citation.

**Published since late 2021**

| Study | Publication | Samples |
|---|---|---|
| [Pediatric Pan-Cancer, MAPPYACTS Trial (Gustave Roussy)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=pancan_mappyacts_2022) | Cancer Discov 2022 | 786 |
| [Pediatric Pancan Tumors (MSK)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=mixed_kunga_msk_2022) | Nat Commun 2022 | 135 |
| [Pediatric Neuroblastoma (MSK)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=nbl_msk_2023) | Nat Genet 2023 | 223 |
| [Pediatric Rhabdomyosarcomas (MSK)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=rms_msk_2023) | JCO Precis Oncol 2023 | 24 |
| [Pediatric solid tumor PDXs (UTHSA)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=pancan_pdx_uthsa_2023) | Nat Commun 2023 | 136 |
| [Pediatric Acute Myeloid Leukemia (St. Jude)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=aml_stjude_2024) | Nat Genet 2024 | 887 |
| [Pediatric Tumors, Make An Impact (MSK)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=pancan_ped_mai_msk_2025) | 2025, no citation listed | 60 |

**TARGET GDC re-processed datasets (2025)**

These carry a 2025 label in their titles but have no associated publication or PMID. Their titles don't say "pediatric", but TARGET is the NCI's childhood-cancer program.
- [Acute Leukemias of Ambiguous Lineage](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=alal_target_gdc): 251 samples
- [Acute Myeloid Leukemia](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=aml_target_gdc): 2,766 samples
- [B-Lymphoblastic Leukemia/Lymphoma](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=bll_target_gdc): 989 samples
- [Neuroblastoma](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=nbl_target_gdc): 533 samples
- [Osteosarcoma](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=os_target_gdc): 159 samples
- [Wilms' Tumor](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=wt_target_gdc): 132 samples

**Just outside the window**
- [Pediatric Low-Grade Glioma (CTF, Acta Neuropathol 2021)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=lgg_ctf_synodos_2025) has 31 samples. By its PubMed ID it appeared in February 2021, so it falls just outside five years. I'd include it if you count by calendar year.
- Older pediatric studies are excluded:
  - Brain CPTAC/CHOP, 2020
  - PPTC, 2019
  - TARGET 2018 cohorts
  - DKFZ pan-cancer, 2017/2018
  - Columbia pan-cancer, 2016
  - Ewing sarcoma, 2014

The portal's import dates all fall in 2026 (re-imports), so they don't reflect publication dates. Sample counts are per study, and the cohorts may overlap (for example, TARGET GDC and the TARGET 2018 studies).

# Sample and Study Filtering Guide

## Overview
Proper filtering is essential for meaningful cBioPortal analysis. This guide covers filtering by studies, sample types, and other criteria.

## Study-Level Filtering

### 1. Always Filter by Study
Every query should specify a study to ensure consistent results:

```sql
-- Always include study filtering
SELECT *
FROM your_table
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    -- Additional filters...
```

### 2. Find Available Studies

```sql
-- Discover available studies
SELECT
    cancer_study_identifier,
    name,
    description,
    type_of_cancer_id
FROM cancer_study
ORDER BY cancer_study_identifier;
```

### 3. Study Information

```sql
-- Get detailed study information
SELECT
    cs.cancer_study_identifier,
    cs.name as study_name,
    cs.description,
    cs.sample_count,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.internal_id) as patient_count
FROM cancer_study cs
LEFT JOIN patient p ON cs.cancer_study_id = p.cancer_study_id
WHERE
    cs.cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
GROUP BY cs.cancer_study_identifier, cs.name, cs.description, cs.sample_count;
```

### 4. Find Studies by Available Data Types

Use this when the user asks *"which studies have mutation and copy-number data for X"*, *"studies with expression for Y"*, *"is there any imaging data"*, or any *"studies with Z data"* question. `cancer_study` has one precomputed sample count per data type — filter on them. question.question: write me python code that can query the timeline files for msk-chord
question.notes:
A correct answer must: write code against the public cBioPortal REST API (e.g. /api/studies/{studyId}/clinical-events).
Must not: write code that needs direct ClickHouse credentials.

reply.answer:
I'll check the msk_chord study ID and how its timeline data is organized, so the code matches the real data.This is Python for both ways of getting the MSK-CHORD (`msk_chord_2024`) timeline data. I haven't run either one, and I wrote the file names and the study-level API endpoint from memory.

- **Option A** reads the `data_timeline_*.txt` files from a local download of the study.
- **Option B** queries the public cBioPortal REST API, so you don't need to download anything.

The study has these timeline event types: `Treatment`, `Diagnosis`, `Lab_Test`, `Pathology`, `Surgery`, `Sequencing` and `Sample acquisition`. All dates are days from diagnosis.

## Option A: local timeline files

Download the study from the [cBioPortal datasets page](https://www.cbioportal.org/datasets) or the DataHub repo. Then point `STUDY_DIR` at the folder.

```python
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

STUDY_DIR = Path("msk_chord_2024")   # folder containing data_timeline_*.txt


def load_timelines(study_dir: Path = STUDY_DIR) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read every data_timeline_*.txt file into one long DataFrame."""
    frames = []
    for f in sorted(study_dir.glob("data_timeline*.txt")):
        df = pd.read_csv(f, sep="\t", dtype=str, low_memory=False)
        df["SOURCE_FILE"] = f.name
        frames.append(df)
    if not frames:
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"No data_timeline*.txt files in {study_dir}")
    tl = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)
    for col in ("START_DATE", "STOP_DATE"):
        if col in tl:
            tl[col] = pd.to_numeric(tl[col], errors="coerce")
    return tl


tl = load_timelines()

# --- Overview -------------------------------------------------------------
print(tl["EVENT_TYPE"].value_counts())
print(tl.groupby("SOURCE_FILE")["PATIENT_ID"].nunique())

# --- Treatment events: agent + category ------------------------------------
tx = tl[tl["EVENT_TYPE"].str.upper() == "TREATMENT"]
print(tx.groupby("AGENT")["PATIENT_ID"].nunique()
        .sort_values(ascending=False).head(20))

# Chemo only
chemo = tx[tx["SUBTYPE"] == "Chemo"]

# --- One patient's timeline ------------------------------------------------
def patient_timeline(patient_id: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    cols = [c for c in ("EVENT_TYPE", "START_DATE", "STOP_DATE", "SUBTYPE", "AGENT")
            if c in tl.columns]
    return (tl[tl["PATIENT_ID"] == patient_id]
            .sort_values("START_DATE")[cols])

# --- Treatments that started before sequencing ----------------------------
seq = (tl[tl["EVENT_TYPE"] == "Sequencing"]
       .groupby("PATIENT_ID")["START_DATE"].min().rename("SEQ_DATE"))
tx_seq = tx.join(seq, on="PATIENT_ID")
pre_seq = tx_seq[tx_seq["START_DATE"] < tx_seq["SEQ_DATE"]]
print(pre_seq.groupby("AGENT")["PATIENT_ID"].nunique()
             .sort_values(ascending=False).head(20))
```

## Option B: public REST API

```python
import requests
import pandas as pd

BASE = "https://www.cbioportal.org/api"
STUDY_ID = "msk_chord_2024"
HEADERS = {"Accept": "application/json"}
# For a private portal, add: HEADERS["Authorization"] = "Bearer <token>"


def events_to_df(events: list[dict]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    rows = []
    for e in events:
        row = {
            "patientId": e.get("patientId"),
            "eventType": e.get("eventType"),
            "start": e.get("startNumberOfDaysSinceDiagnosis"),
            "stop": e.get("endNumberOfDaysSinceDiagnosis"),
        }
        # attributes come back as [{"key": "AGENT", "value": "..."}, ...]
        row.update({a["key"]: a["value"] for a in e.get("attributes", [])})
        rows.append(row)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def get_patient_events(patient_id: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """All timeline events for a single patient."""
    url = f"{BASE}/studies/{STUDY_ID}/patients/{patient_id}/clinical-events"
    r = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, params={"projection": "DETAILED"}, timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return events_to_df(r.json())


def get_study_events(page_size: int = 10000, max_pages: int | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Study-wide events, paged. MSK-CHORD has millions of events, so
    limit pages while testing."""
    url = f"{BASE}/studies/{STUDY_ID}/clinical-events"
    frames, page = [], 0
    while max_pages is None or page < max_pages:
        r = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=120,
                         params={"projection": "DETAILED",
                                 "pageSize": page_size, "pageNumber": page})
        r.raise_for_status()
        batch = r.json()
        if not batch:
            break
        frames.append(events_to_df(batch))
        page += 1
    return pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True) if frames else pd.DataFrame()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Sample the first 5 pages to check the structure
    df = get_study_events(page_size=5000, max_pages=5)
    print(df["eventType"].value_counts())

    tx = df[df["eventType"].str.upper() == "TREATMENT"]
    print(tx.groupby("AGENT")["patientId"].nunique()
            .sort_values(ascending=False).head(10))
```

## Notes

- **Treatment fields:** treatment events carry `AGENT`, `SUBTYPE`, `RX_INVESTIGATIVE`, `FLAG_OROTOPICAL`, and (for NLP-derived prior medications) `PRIOR_MED_TO_MSK` and `INFERRED_TX_PROB`. Filter on these if you want to exclude investigational or prior-to-MSK drugs.
- **Event-type casing:** I match `Treatment` case-insensitively because some studies use `TREATMENT`.
- **Counts:** report patient counts rather than percentages. The data can't separate "never received" from "not recorded".
- **Size:** the study has well over a million timeline events, mostly `Diagnosis` rows. In the API version, pass `max_pages` or filter by patient first. In the file version, you can use `usecols=` or read only the treatment file to save memory.
- **Check the files first:** run `print(sorted(STUDY_DIR.glob("data_timeline*")))` to confirm your download's file names. If the study-level endpoint isn't available on your portal version, loop `get_patient_events` over patient IDs.

I can also adapt this to a specific question, such as treatment sequences or time from sequencing to first immunotherapy. I can also build a cBioPortal link for a cohort you want to look at.

# Treatment Data Query Guide

## Overview

Treatment data in cBioPortal is stored in **clinical event tables**, separate from clinical attributes. This allows for timeline-based treatment records with start/stop dates.

## Start Here: Treatment Views

For "most common treatments / agents / regimens in study X", use the parameterized views (documented in `cbioportal://clinical-data-guide`, Study-View Chart Counts):

```sql
-- Patients per agent (the portal's Treatment chart), with type/subtype arrays
SELECT * FROM treatment_counts_in_study(study='msk_chord_2024') ORDER BY patients DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Same-day agent combinations (investigational, prior-medication and radiation events excluded)
SELECT * FROM treatment_regimens_in_study(study='msk_chord_2024') ORDER BY patients DESC LIMIT 20;
```

Write raw event queries (below) only for subgroups, timelines or keys the views do not expose.

## Key Tables

| Table | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `clinical_event` | Event records with patient_id, event_type, start_date, stop_date |
| `clinical_event_data` | Key-value pairs linked to each clinical_event_id |

## Schema

```
clinical_event
├── clinical_event_id (PK)
├── patient_id (FK → patient.internal_id)
├── event_type (Treatment, TREATMENT, Diagnosis, SURGERY, etc.)
├── start_date (days from diagnosis)

# Sample and Study Filtering Guide

## Overview
Proper filtering is essential for meaningful cBioPortal analysis. This guide covers filtering by studies, sample types, and other criteria.

## Study-Level Filtering

### 1. Always Filter by Study
Every query should specify a study to ensure consistent results:

```sql
-- Always include study filtering
SELECT *
FROM your_table
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    -- Additional filters...
```

### 2. Find Available Studies

```sql
-- Discover available studies
SELECT
    cancer_study_identifier,
    name,
    description,
    type_of_cancer_id
FROM cancer_study
ORDER BY cancer_study_identifier;
```

### 3. Study Information

```sql
-- Get detailed study information
SELECT
    cs.cancer_study_identifier,
    cs.name as study_name,
    cs.description,
    cs.sample_count,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.internal_id) as patient_count
FROM cancer_study cs
LEFT JOIN patient p ON cs.cancer_study_id = p.cancer_study_id
WHERE
    cs.cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
GROUP BY cs.cancer_study_identifier, cs.name, cs.description, cs.sample_count;
```

### 4. Find Studies by Available Data Types

Use this when the user asks *"which studies have mutation and copy-number data for X"*, *"studies with expression for Y"*, *"is there any imaging data"*, or any *"studies with Z data"* question. `cancer_study` has one precomputed sample count per data type — filter on them. reply.answer:
# Drivers in adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) and BCOR

**Data source:** Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma Project (J Clin Invest 2019, `acc_2019`). I restricted it to the 935 samples (931 patients) coded as ACYC. The study also contains lung and breast ACC samples. Frequencies are per sample, and all 935 were profiled for mutations. The actionability tiers below come from general knowledge, not from cBioPortal data. They are not clinical advice, and I didn't check them against OncoKB, guidelines or the literature.

## Most frequent alterations in this cohort

| Alteration | Samples | % of 935 |
|---|---|---|
| **MYB structural variant (fusion)** | 163 | 17.4% |
| **NFIB structural variant (fusion)** | 152 | 16.3% |
| MYBL1 structural variant | 7 | 0.7% |
| **NOTCH1 mutation** | 211 | 22.6% |
| KDM6A mutation | 129 | 13.8% |
| ARID1A mutation | 105 | 11.2% |
| KMT2D mutation | 98 | 10.5% |
| **BCOR mutation** | 95 | 10.2% |
| KMT2C mutation | 86 | 9.2% |
| CREBBP mutation | 84 | 9.0% |
| TERT mutation | 75 | 8.0% |
| ARID1B mutation | 70 | 7.5% |
| EP300 mutation | 68 | 7.3% |
| TP53 mutation | 66 | 7.1% |
| SPEN mutation | 61 | 6.5% |
| PIK3CA mutation | 51 | 5.5% |
| PTEN mutation | 21 | 2.2% |
| CDKN2A deep deletion | 26 | 2.8% |

- MYB and NFIB are both partners of the canonical MYB::NFIB fusion, so these two counts overlap. I didn't compute the number of samples with either.
- The structural variant percentages use all 935 samples as the denominator. The structural variant profiling denominator may be smaller.
- The TERT figure counts all TERT mutation records, not specifically promoter mutations, because I couldn't separate them here.
- Many of the other mutations, such as BRCA2, ATM and LRP1B, are probably passengers. Frequently mutated does not mean oncogenic, and no driver annotation is stored for this study.

## Classification by actionability (general knowledge, not from the database)

**Tier 1: defining drivers, no approved matched therapy**
- MYB::NFIB, MYB and MYBL1 fusions and rearrangements are the hallmark ACC alteration. They are diagnostically useful but are not directly targetable.

**Tier 2: potentially actionable or trial-relevant**
- NOTCH1 activating mutations are a marker of a more aggressive, solid-pattern disease. They are the target of Notch-inhibitor trials, such as AL101 (γ-secretase inhibitor).
- PIK3CA and PTEN alterations, and other PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway changes, are theoretically targetable but have limited ACC-specific evidence.
- NTRK1 (4.0% of samples mutated) is listed as a mutation count only. It is not a confirmed fusion, so it is not actionable on this evidence.

**Tier 3: epigenetic and chromatin regulators, mostly investigational**
- This group includes KDM6A, ARID1A, ARID1B, KMT2C, KMT2D, CREBBP, EP300, SPEN, BCOR and SMARCA2.
- Some are being explored with HDAC, EZH2 or BET inhibitors, but there is no established ACC indication.

**Tier 4: prognostic or biological context only**
- TP53 mutations and CDKN2A/CDKN2B deletions are mostly associated with high-grade transformation and worse outcome.

## BCOR

**Somatic:** BCOR is mutated in 95 of 935 samples (10.2%), which makes it one of the most frequently mutated genes in this cohort.
- Among the 101 BCOR mutation records, 38 are frameshift deletions and 31 are frameshift insertions.
- There are also 18 nonsense, 12 missense and 2 splice-site mutations, plus 2 flagged as targeted-region.
- That is about 88% truncating, consistent with loss of function. BCOR is X-linked.
- One sample has a BCOR deep deletion.
- BCOR also appears in the other ACC studies, but only once each in the MDA 2015 and MSK 2013 studies.
- I did not test whether BCOR mutations are associated with outcome or with co-occurring alterations.

**Germline:** None of the 8 ACC-related studies in cBioPortal contains any variant labelled germline. All BCOR calls in `acc_2019` are labelled somatic. Germline BCOR status therefore can't be assessed here, and this absence of germline calls says nothing about whether any BCOR variants are inherited.

From general knowledge, not from cBioPortal: germline BCOR loss-of-function variants cause oculofaciocardiodental syndrome. ACC predisposition has not been established for BCOR carriers.

## Links
- [OncoPrint of MYB, NFIB, NOTCH1, BCOR, KDM6A, ARID1A, CREBBP, TP53, PIK3CA, PTEN and CDKN2A in ACYC samples](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/oncoprint?session_id=6b06da0a5b3de0d55f916ac7)
- [Filtered study view of the ACYC cohort](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=acc_2019#filterJson=%7B%22clinicalDataFilters%22%3A%5B%7B%22attributeId%22%3A%22ONCOTREE_CODE%22%2C%22values%22%3A%5B%7B%22value%22%3A%22ACYC%22%7D%5D%7D%5D%7D)

Other ACC studies, which are smaller: [MDA 2015](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=acyc_mda_2015), [MSK 2013](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=acyc_mskcc_2013), [FMI 2014](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=acyc_fmi_2014), [JHU 2016](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=acyc_jhu_2016), [Sanger/MDA 2013](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=acyc_sanger_2013), [MGH 2016](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=acyc_mgh_2016).

tool_calls.result:
# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)

Germline Variant Guide
======================

Overview
--------
cBioPortal stores both somatic AND germline variant data. Many cBioPortal features work identically for both variant types. This guide explains how to query germline variants and what to be aware of.

How Germline Data is Stored
---------------------------

### mutation_status is free text — always compare case-insensitively
Each study loads its own spelling. Germline calls appear as `'Germline'`, `'GERMLINE'` and `'germline'`; somatic calls as `'Somatic'`, `'SOMATIC'` and `'somatic'`; unannotated mutations as `'NA'`, `'.'`, `'Unknown'`, `'UNKNOWN'`, `'__UNKNOWN__'` and others. Matching one spelling silently drops whole studies (`mutation_status = 'Germline'` misses `all_stjude_2013`, `aml_stjude_2024` and `pog570_bcgsc_2020`).

- **Germline:** `upper(mutation_status) = 'GERMLINE'`
- **Somatic:** `upper(mutation_status) = 'SOMATIC'` — but only when the user asks for somatic-only. Many studies label their somatic calls `'NA'` or `'UNKNOWN'`, so for ordinary mutation questions follow common-pitfalls #3 and exclude only `'UNCALLED'`.

# Sample and Study Filtering Guide

## Overview
Proper filtering is essential for meaningful cBioPortal analysis. This guide covers filtering by studies, sample types, and other criteria.

## Study-Level Filtering

### 1. Always Filter by Study
Every query should specify a study to ensure consistent results:

```sql
-- Always include study filtering
SELECT *
FROM your_table
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    -- Additional filters...
```

### 2. Find Available Studies

```sql
-- Discover available studies
SELECT
    cancer_study_identifier,
    name,
    description,
    type_of_cancer_id
FROM cancer_study
ORDER BY cancer_study_identifier;
```

### 3. Study Information

```sql
-- Get detailed study information
SELECT
    cs.cancer_study_identifier,
    cs.name as study_name,
    cs.description,
    cs.sample_count,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.internal_id) as patient_count
FROM cancer_study cs
LEFT JOIN patient p ON cs.cancer_study_id = p.cancer_study_id
WHERE
    cs.cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
GROUP BY cs.cancer_study_identifier, cs.name, cs.description, cs.sample_count;
```

# cBioPortal FAQ Guide

Curated answers to frequently asked general questions about cBioPortal. Source: [cBioPortal FAQ](https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/).

## What is cBioPortal?

cBioPortal for Cancer Genomics is an open-access, open-source resource for interactive exploration of multidimensional cancer genomics data sets. It was originally developed at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) and is now maintained by a multi-institutional team.

## History

- **2008**: cBioPortal first became available online.
- **2012**: First major publication — Cerami et al., *Cancer Discovery*.
- **2013**: Second major publication — Gao et al., *Science Signaling*.
- **2023**: Third major publication — de Bruijn et al., *Cancer Research*.

## How to Cite cBioPortal

When using cBioPortal in publications, cite these three papers:

1. Cerami et al. "The cBio Cancer Genomics Portal: An Open Platform for Exploring Multidimensional Cancer Genomics Data." *Cancer Discovery* 2, 401–404 (2012). doi:10.1158/2159-8290.CD-12-0095
2. Gao et al. "Integrative Analysis of Complex Cancer Genomics and Clinical Profiles Using the cBioPortal." *Science Signaling* 6, pl1 (2013). doi:10.1126/scisignal.2004088
3. de Bruijn et al. "Analysis and Visualization of Longitudinal Genomic and Clinical Data from the AACR Project GENIE Biopharma Collaborative in cBioPortal." *Cancer Research* 83, 3861–3867 (2023). doi:10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-23-0816

question.question: I receive a report with the PIK3CA p.*1069Wext*3 mutation. Can you provide details of it
question.notes:
A correct answer must: report cBioPortal counts of the variant (and OncoKB annotation if available) and say that biological significance needs external sources (OncoKB, literature).

reply.answer:
**I found no PIK3CA p.\*1069Wext\*3 in the database. The closest match is p.\*1069Wext\*4.**

**What the notation means**
- PIK3CA's normal protein ends at residue 1068. Position 1069 is the stop codon.
- The change turns the stop codon (\*) into tryptophan (W). The protein is then extended until the next stop codon. That is a stop-loss (nonstop) mutation.
- The "\*3" or "\*4" is how many residues the new tail runs before a new stop is reached. Your report says \*3. cBioPortal records \*4.
- The two may be the same event written with different counting, or two different events. I can't tell which from this data. Please check the exact HGVS/transcript notation with the lab that issued the report.

**Closest match: PIK3CA \*1069Wext\*4 (Nonstop_Mutation)**
I counted unique patients with this variant. These are raw occurrence counts only, with no frequency calculation.

| Cohort | Patients | Cancer type |
|---|---|---|
| MSK-IMPACT 50K (`msk_impact_50k_2026`) | 3 | Colon adenocarcinoma, uterine endometrioid carcinoma, high-grade serous ovarian cancer |
| MSK-CHORD 2024 | 2 | Colon adenocarcinoma (both) |
| MSK-MET 2021 | 2 | Colon adenocarcinoma, uterine endometrioid carcinoma |
| MSK pan-cancer MIMSI 2024 | 2 | Colon adenocarcinoma, uterine endometrioid carcinoma |
| CRC MSK 2026 | 2 | Colon adenocarcinoma (both) |
| TCGA GBM (several versions of the same study) | 1 | Glioblastoma, sample TCGA-32-1979-01 |
| METABRIC | 1 | Breast invasive ductal carcinoma |
| CRC DFCI 2016 | 1 | Colorectal adenocarcinoma |
| Cell lines: CCLE (IGROV1 ovary, KYSE70 oesophagus), NCI-60 | Not counted | Cell lines, not patients |

- The MSK studies overlap heavily and share the same patients. The two colon cases (P-0038429, P-0077592), the uterine case (P-0029972) and the ovarian case (P-0067686) each appear in several MSK cohorts. The TCGA GBM case also appears in several TCGA versions. So there are only about 8–9 distinct patient tumors in total. Please don't add up the table rows.
- None of these studies has driver or oncogenicity annotation in the database.

**Neighbouring variants at the same stop codon**
- \*1069Ffs\*5, a frameshift: several MSK and breast cohorts.
- \*1069Lfs\*4/\*5 and \*1069fs\*: single cases.
- Other nonstop calls at \*1064, \*1068, \*1069 and \*1069Rext\*4: a few cases.

**What cBioPortal can't tell you**
Counts of occurrences don't show whether this variant matters biologically or clinically. For that, check an external curated source such as OncoKB, ClinVar or UniProt, or the primary literature. I didn't review any of those here. I can't offer clinical interpretation.

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.
- **For "across cancer types" questions**, jump to the [Cross-Cancer-Type Mutation Frequency](#cross-cancer-type-mutation-frequency) section below — there is one correct recipe and several common wrong ones.

Before answering any mutation count or frequency question, decide whether the unit is samples or patients and state that choice in the answer.

| User wording | Counting unit |

```sql

question.notes:

reply.answer:
I couldn't confirm that any study has a file named `data_clinical_outcomes.txt`. My database holds the loaded data, not the original upload files or their names, so I can't see file names.

I also don't think cBioPortal has a standard file by that name. The documented clinical formats are:

- `data_clinical_patient.txt` with `meta_clinical_patient.txt`
- `data_clinical_sample.txt` with `meta_clinical_sample.txt`
- `data_timeline_<name>.txt` with `meta_timeline_<name>.txt`

Outcome data is normally loaded in one of two ways:

1. **Patient file:** outcome columns such as `OS_STATUS`, `OS_MONTHS`, `DFS_STATUS` and `PFS_STATUS` sit in the patient clinical file.
2. **Timeline file:** outcome events such as status, progression or recurrence sit in a timeline file.

If a collaborator or tutorial told you to use `data_clinical_outcomes.txt`, it may be a custom name from a private study package. You can name the file anything as long as the meta file's `data_filename` points to it. The meta file for a clinical data file uses `genetic_alteration_type: CLINICAL` and `datatype: PATIENT_ATTRIBUTES`. A timeline file uses `datatype: TIMELINE`.

## Studies to emulate
**Outcome columns in the patient file**
- [Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018) (`brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018`): 1,084 patients have `OS_STATUS`, `DFS_STATUS` and `PFS_STATUS`. The other PanCancer Atlas TCGA studies have the same layout. This is the standard template.
- [Rectal cancer (MSK, 2022)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=rectal_msk_2022) (`rectal_msk_2022`): curated outcome and response attributes, including `RECURRENCE`, `LOCAL_RECURRENCE`, `DISTAL_RECURRENCE`, `LARC_CRT_OUTCOME_CASES_DFS`, `RESPONSE_PCR_OR_CCR` and `USE_IN_OUTCOME_ANALYSIS`.
- [Gastroesophageal cancer, TRAP (MSK, 2023)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=egc_trap_ccr_msk_2023) (`egc_trap_ccr_msk_2023`): treatment response and recurrence attributes, including `BEST_RESPONSE_CATEGORY` and `9_WEEK_RECIST_RESPONSE`.
- [Bladder, BCAN HCRN (2022)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=blca_bcan_hcrn_2022) (`blca_bcan_hcrn_2022`): best response by therapy class, such as `BEST_RESPONSE_IMMUNOTHERAPY`.

**Outcome or status as timeline events**
- [MSK MetTropism (MSK, Cell 2021)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=msk_met_2021) (`msk_met_2021`): about 25,700 `STATUS` events with deceased or living values. This is a good template for a status timeline.
- [Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018): the same study also has `STATUS` timeline events. They cover vital status, tumor status and staging at initial diagnosis, so it shows both approaches.

## Getting the actual files
Every study in the public portal has a downloadable package. Open it and look at the file names and meta files directly:

`https://datahub.assets.cbioportal.org/<study_id>.tar.gz`

For example: `https://datahub.assets.cbioportal.org/rectal_msk_2022.tar.gz`

If you tell me what the outcomes file should contain, I can pick the closest study and list its outcome attributes with patient counts. Examples would be survival only, recurrence, or treatment response with dates. If you want the timeline route, I can also show which event types and keys a study uses.

# cBioPortal FAQ Guide

Curated answers to frequently asked general questions about cBioPortal. Source: [cBioPortal FAQ](https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/).

## What is cBioPortal?

cBioPortal for Cancer Genomics is an open-access, open-source resource for interactive exploration of multidimensional cancer genomics data sets. It was originally developed at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) and is now maintained by a multi-institutional team.

## History

- **2008**: cBioPortal first became available online.
- **2012**: First major publication — Cerami et al., *Cancer Discovery*.
- **2013**: Second major publication — Gao et al., *Science Signaling*.
- **2023**: Third major publication — de Bruijn et al., *Cancer Research*.

## How to Cite cBioPortal

When using cBioPortal in publications, cite these three papers:

1. Cerami et al. "The cBio Cancer Genomics Portal: An Open Platform for Exploring Multidimensional Cancer Genomics Data." *Cancer Discovery* 2, 401–404 (2012). doi:10.1158/2159-8290.CD-12-0095
2. Gao et al. "Integrative Analysis of Complex Cancer Genomics and Clinical Profiles Using the cBioPortal." *Science Signaling* 6, pl1 (2013). doi:10.1126/scisignal.2004088
3. de Bruijn et al. "Analysis and Visualization of Longitudinal Genomic and Clinical Data from the AACR Project GENIE Biopharma Collaborative in cBioPortal." *Cancer Research* 83, 3861–3867 (2023). doi:10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-23-0816

# MSK-CHORD (MSK, Nature 2024)

**Study ID:** `msk_chord_2024`

## Overview
Targeted sequencing via MSK-IMPACT panels. Clinical annotations include some derived from natural language processing (denoted NLP).

**Exactly five cancer types** (`CANCER_TYPE`, patients): Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 7,809, Colorectal Cancer 5,543, Breast Cancer 5,368, Prostate Cancer 3,211, Pancreatic Cancer 3,109. question.notes:

reply.answer:
A good example is **Metastatic Breast Cancer (AURORA US Network, Nat Cancer 2023)**, study ID `brca_aurora_2023`. It has 155 samples and a clinical timeline for each patient. The timeline records Diagnosis, Treatment, Specimen, Follow-up and Surgery events.

**Patient with many samples over time: AUR-AFE5**
- This patient has 10 samples: one primary tumor and nine metastatic samples.
- The samples are `AUR_01_15_01`, `_03`, `_04`, `_06`, `_07`, `_08`, `_09`, `_10`, `_11` and `_12`.
- The patient has 26 timeline events.

[Open patient AUR-AFE5](https://www.cbioportal.org/patient/summary?studyId=brca_aurora_2023&caseId=AUR-AFE5)

**A simpler alternative: AUR-AER2**
- This patient has 3 samples: one primary tumor and two metastatic samples (`AUR_01_07_01`, `_03` and `_05`).
- The patient has 42 timeline events, so the treatment and surgery history is easy to read.

[Open patient AUR-AER2](https://www.cbioportal.org/patient/summary?studyId=brca_aurora_2023&caseId=AUR-AER2)

On the patient page, the timeline at the top shows when each sample was taken relative to treatments and other events. Below it, the mutation and copy-number tables let you compare samples from the same patient.

**Other studies with sample and treatment timelines**
- [MSK-CHORD (MSK, Nature 2024)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=msk_chord_2024) has about 25,000 patients with timeline events.
- [The Metastatic Breast Cancer Project (Provisional, December 2021)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=brca_mbcproject_2022) has 253 patients with timeline events. One example is `MBCProject_ePi1smiM`, who has 5 samples and 21 timeline events.
- [Pan-cancer Analysis of Organoid Samples (HCMI, 2025)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=pancan_hcmi_2025) has 637 patients with timeline events.

You can also browse the [AURORA study overview](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=brca_aurora_2023).

# Sample and Study Filtering Guide

## Overview
Proper filtering is essential for meaningful cBioPortal analysis. This guide covers filtering by studies, sample types, and other criteria.

## Study-Level Filtering

### 1. Always Filter by Study
Every query should specify a study to ensure consistent results:

```sql
-- Always include study filtering
SELECT *
FROM your_table
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    -- Additional filters...
```

### 2. Find Available Studies

```sql
-- Discover available studies
SELECT
    cancer_study_identifier,
    name,
    description,
    type_of_cancer_id
FROM cancer_study
ORDER BY cancer_study_identifier;
```

### 3. Study Information

```sql
-- Get detailed study information
SELECT
    cs.cancer_study_identifier,
    cs.name as study_name,
    cs.description,
    cs.sample_count,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.internal_id) as patient_count
FROM cancer_study cs
LEFT JOIN patient p ON cs.cancer_study_id = p.cancer_study_id
WHERE
    cs.cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
GROUP BY cs.cancer_study_identifier, cs.name, cs.description, cs.sample_count;
```

### 4. Find Studies by Available Data Types

Use this when the user asks *"which studies have mutation and copy-number data for X"*, *"studies with expression for Y"*, *"is there any imaging data"*, or any *"studies with Z data"* question. `cancer_study` has one precomputed sample count per data type — filter on them. # Sample and Study Filtering Guide

## Overview
Proper filtering is essential for meaningful cBioPortal analysis. This guide covers filtering by studies, sample types, and other criteria.

## Study-Level Filtering

### 1. Always Filter by Study
Every query should specify a study to ensure consistent results:

```sql
-- Always include study filtering
SELECT *
FROM your_table
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    -- Additional filters...
```

### 2. Find Available Studies

```sql
-- Discover available studies
SELECT
    cancer_study_identifier,
    name,
    description,
    type_of_cancer_id
FROM cancer_study
ORDER BY cancer_study_identifier;
```

### 3. Study Information

```sql
-- Get detailed study information
SELECT
    cs.cancer_study_identifier,
    cs.name as study_name,
    cs.description,
    cs.sample_count,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.internal_id) as patient_count
FROM cancer_study cs
LEFT JOIN patient p ON cs.cancer_study_id = p.cancer_study_id
WHERE
    cs.cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
GROUP BY cs.cancer_study_identifier, cs.name, cs.description, cs.sample_count;
```

### 4. Find Studies by Available Data Types

Use this when the user asks *"which studies have mutation and copy-number data for X"*, *"studies with expression for Y"*, *"is there any imaging data"*, or any *"studies with Z data"* question. `cancer_study` has one precomputed sample count per data type — filter on them. question.question: Can you explore the difference in mutation frequency between left-sided and right-sided CRC?
question.notes:
A correct answer must: explain that left vs right sidedness is defined by the splenic flexure (not colon vs rectum), use sub-site annotations where a study has them, or say the data doesn't support the comparison.
Must not: substitute a colon-vs-rectum comparison.

reply.answer:
I'll start by reading the relevant guides and finding the colorectal studies.Several colorectal studies match. Next I'll check which ones record tumor sidedness.The TCGA PanCancer Atlas study has the subsite data needed to derive sidedness. The large MSK 2026 study may have it too, so I'll look at both.TCGA PanCancer Atlas is the cleanest cohort here. It is exome-sequenced, so every gene has the same denominator, and the ICD-O-3 subsite codes let me assign sidedness. I'll start with that cohort.# Mutation frequency in left-sided vs right-sided colorectal cancer

I used the [TCGA PanCancer Atlas colorectal cohort](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=coadread_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018). It is exome-sequenced, so every gene has the same denominator. Sidedness is not recorded directly, so I derived it from the ICD-O-3 tumor subsite code.

- **Right:** cecum, ascending colon and hepatic flexure.
- **Left:** splenic flexure, descending colon, sigmoid, rectosigmoid and rectum.
- **Excluded:** transverse colon (20 patients) and colon NOS (97), because their side is ambiguous.

The unit is patients with mutation data. That gives 170 right-sided and 254 left-sided patients.

## Selected genes

| Gene | Right-sided | Left-sided | Left − Right (points) |
|---|---|---|---|
| BRAF | 40/170 (23.5%) | 10/254 (3.9%) | −19.6 |
| PIK3CA | 62/170 (36.5%) | 45/254 (17.7%) | −18.8 |
| RNF43 | 33/170 (19.4%) | 7/254 (2.8%) | −16.6 |
| KRAS | 82/170 (48.2%) | 83/254 (32.7%) | −15.5 |
| SOX9 | 29/170 (17.1%) | 18/254 (7.1%) | −10.0 |
| ARID1A | 25/170 (14.7%) | 17/254 (6.7%) | −8.0 |
| ACVR2A | 21/170 (12.4%) | 9/254 (3.5%) | −8.9 |
| TP53 | 88/170 (51.8%) | 174/254 (68.5%) | +16.7 |
| APC | 112/170 (65.9%) | 199/254 (78.3%) | +12.4 |
| SMAD4 | 25/170 (14.7%) | 29/254 (11.4%) | −3.3 |
| FBXW7 | 30/170 (17.6%) | 37/254 (14.6%) | −3.0 |
| NRAS | 10/170 (5.9%) | 19/254 (7.5%) | +1.6 |

Beyond this list, the largest gaps across all genes were in large genes such as PCLO, KMT2D, TTN, LRP2 and ZFHX4. These were all higher on the right.

## Hypermutation confounds the comparison

Right-sided tumors in this cohort are much more often hypermutated (MSI or POLE subtypes). I counted 46 of 191 right-sided patients versus 12 of 280 left-sided. Hypermutation inflates mutation rates in large and passenger-prone genes. That likely explains much of the broad right-sided excess in genes like PCLO and TTN.

I repeated the comparison in non-hypermutated tumors only (124 right, 242 left):

| Gene | Right (non-hypermutated) | Left (non-hypermutated) |
|---|---|---|
| KRAS | 69/124 (55.6%) | 77/242 (31.8%) |
| PIK3CA | 44/124 (35.5%) | 38/242 (15.7%) |
| SOX9 | 21/124 (16.9%) | 16/242 (6.6%) |
| BRAF | 13/124 (10.5%) | 5/242 (2.1%) |
| TP53 | 75/124 (60.5%) | 167/242 (69.0%) |
| APC | 94/124 (75.8%) | 189/242 (78.1%) |
| RNF43 | 7/124 (5.6%) | 5/242 (2.1%) |

- **Hypermutation explains part of the pattern.** The RNF43 gap shrinks to about 3.5 points. The APC gap shrinks to about 2 points. The TP53 gap narrows from 16.7 to about 8.5 points.
- **Some right-sided differences persist.** KRAS, PIK3CA and SOX9 remain higher on the right in non-hypermutated tumors, and BRAF stays higher but with small counts.

## Caveats

- I haven't tested whether these differences are statistically significant. The appropriate test is Fisher's exact test with multiple-testing correction. The Group Comparison link below runs it for every gene.
- Hypermutation is defined here by TCGA's MSI and POLE molecular subtypes.
- Mutations only. Copy-number and structural events aren't included.

## Links

- [Right vs left alteration comparison](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/alterations?comparisonId=6b06da4ed69ab756cb916ac8): the same two groups, with enrichment statistics for all genes. The groups contain 191 and 280 patients, which includes some without mutation data. The tables above use only the 170 and 254 with mutation data.
- [Study overview](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=coadread_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018)

A larger cohort is available if you'd like to check these findings. The MSK 2026 colorectal study (`crc_msk_2026`, about 7,200 samples) records primary subsite. It is targeted-panel sequenced, so the denominators vary by gene. I can repeat the analysis there.

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.
- **For "across cancer types" questions**, jump to the [Cross-Cancer-Type Mutation Frequency](#cross-cancer-type-mutation-frequency) section below — there is one correct recipe and several common wrong ones.

## Counting Unit: Samples vs Patients

Before answering any mutation count or frequency question, decide whether the unit is samples or patients and state that choice in the answer.

| User wording | Counting unit |

| "prevalence", "rate", "fraction of patients", "patients with", "how common is" | Patient-level: `COUNT(DISTINCT patient_unique_id)` |

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

# Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

## Recommended Approach: Use clinical_data_derived

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

```sql

SELECT
    sample_unique_id,
    patient_unique_id,
    attribute_name,
    attribute_value
FROM clinical_data_derived
WHERE

question.question: In lower grade glioma, are there genes which are overexpressed in any of the molecular subtypes?
question.notes:
A correct answer must: use an LGG study that has mRNA expression data (e.g. lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018) and link to the group comparison mRNA tab. (Rephrased from a follow-up in an LGG molecular-subtype conversation.)

reply.answer:
Yes, you can test this directly in cBioPortal. I didn't run any statistics myself, so I can't name specific overexpressed genes. The link below opens the test already set up.

[View mRNA expression enrichment across LGG molecular subtypes](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/mrna?comparisonId=6b06da5dd19a2abe92916ac9)

**Cohort:** Brain Lower Grade Glioma (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas). The groups use the study's `SUBTYPE` annotation, which has three subtypes:

| Subtype | Samples |
|---|---|
| LGG_IDHwt | 92 |
| LGG_IDHmut-codel | 167 |
| LGG_IDHmut-non-codel | 248 |

Samples with no subtype annotation (about 7 of the 514) are left out.

**What the page shows:** It compares mRNA expression for every gene across the three subtypes. For each gene it gives the group means and a significance test with FDR correction. Genes that are significantly higher in one subtype than in the others are the overexpressed ones.

**How to use it:**
- To see genes overexpressed in one subtype, select that group and compare it against the others. You can also pick any two groups for a pairwise test.
- Sort by q-value to find the strongest differences. Look at the log ratio as well, because a gene can be significant with only a small difference in expression.
- Expression here is z-scored within this cohort. That makes the values comparable between subtypes but not between cancer types.

**Related views:**

question.question: What are the frequencies of different KRAS mutations in TCGA PanCan Lung Adenocarcinoma?
question.notes:
A correct answer must: link directly to the results view Mutations tab for KRAS in luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018.
Must not: link to OncoPrint and explain how to navigate to Mutations, or add "what you'll find" summaries from background knowledge.

reply.answer:
KRAS mutations by protein change in [Lung Adenocarcinoma (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018). Counts are samples, out of 566 profiled for KRAS.

| KRAS variant | Mutation type | Samples | Frequency |
|---|---|---|---|
| G12C | Missense | 70 | 12.4% |
| G12V | Missense | 40 | 7.1% |
| G12D | Missense | 20 | 3.5% |
| G12A | Missense | 17 | 3.0% |
| G13C | Missense | 7 | 1.2% |
| G12S | Missense | 5 | 0.9% |
| L19F | Missense | 3 | 0.5% |
| G13D | Missense | 3 | 0.5% |
| Q61L | Missense | 3 | 0.5% |
| D33E | Missense | 1 | 0.2% |
| A146P | Missense | 1 | 0.2% |
| Q61H | Missense | 1 | 0.2% |
| K88* | Nonsense | 1 | 0.2% |

- **Codon 12 dominates.** G12C, G12V, G12D, G12A and G12S together account for 152 of the variant calls. That is about 27% of the 566 samples, assuming each sample carries only one KRAS variant.
- **Mutation type.** All variants are missense except K88*, which is a nonsense mutation.
- **Driver status.** These are all somatic KRAS mutations. They are not filtered for oncogenic or driver status. Rare variants such as D33E and L19F may not be drivers.

[Open the KRAS Mutations tab for this study](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/mutations?cancer_study_list=luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&gene_list=KRAS%3A+MUT&case_set_id=luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018_all) to see the lollipop plot and the full mutation table. You can also [explore the study cohort](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018).

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.
- **For "across cancer types" questions**, jump to the [Cross-Cancer-Type Mutation Frequency](#cross-cancer-type-mutation-frequency) section below — there is one correct recipe and several common wrong ones.

## Counting Unit: Samples vs Patients

Before answering any mutation count or frequency question, decide whether the unit is samples or patients and state that choice in the answer.

| User wording | Counting unit |
|--------------|---------------|
| "prevalence", "rate", "fraction of patients", "patients with", "how common is" | Patient-level: `COUNT(DISTINCT patient_unique_id)` |

question.question: Are there DNA methylation differences between lower grade glioma molecular subtypes?
question.notes:
A correct answer must: link to the group comparison DNA methylation tab (probe-level, e.g. cg00000292). (Rephrased from follow-ups.)
Must not: claim group comparison has no methylation tab.

reply.answer:
I can't tell you from the data whether the differences are statistically significant. I haven't run the methylation test, and the database I query can't compute one. The comparison page below will run it and rank probes by differential methylation.

I used the TCGA PanCancer Atlas lower grade glioma study, which has HM450 methylation data. I split the samples by its molecular subtype:

| Subtype | Samples |
|---|---|
| IDH-mutant, 1p/19q-codeleted | 167 |
| IDH-mutant, non-codeleted | 248 |
| IDH wild-type | 92 |

[Open the DNA methylation comparison across the three LGG subtypes](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/generic_assay_methylation?comparisonId=6b06da690e3cf6cc0e916aca)

On that page, probes are ranked by differential methylation (beta values) across the three groups. You can pick two groups for a pairwise comparison, such as IDH-mutant vs IDH wild-type.

Related links:
- [Study overview with the subtype distribution](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018)
- Subtype cohorts: [IDHmut-codel](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018#filterJson=%7B%22clinicalDataFilters%22%3A%5B%7B%22attributeId%22%3A%22SUBTYPE%22%2C%22values%22%3A%5B%7B%22value%22%3A%22LGG_IDHmut-codel%22%7D%5D%7D%5D%7D), [IDHmut-non-codel](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018#filterJson=%7B%22clinicalDataFilters%22%3A%5B%7B%22attributeId%22%3A%22SUBTYPE%22%2C%22values%22%3A%5B%7B%22value%22%3A%22LGG_IDHmut-non-codel%22%7D%5D%7D%5D%7D), [IDHwt](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018#filterJson=%7B%22clinicalDataFilters%22%3A%5B%7B%22attributeId%22%3A%22SUBTYPE%22%2C%22values%22%3A%5B%7B%22value%22%3A%22LGG_IDHwt%22%7D%5D%7D%5D%7D)

Notes:
- The subtype counts add up to 507 of the 514 samples. The other 7 have no subtype recorded and are left out.
- The older Firehose Legacy LGG study (`lgg_tcga`) also has HM450 data. It has no subtype attribute, only an `IDH1_MUTATION` field.

question.question: Are there differences in chromosome arm 7p copy number between lower grade glioma molecular subtypes?
question.notes:
A correct answer must: return a valid link to the group comparison arm-level CNA view (or the copy-number tab), or explain what is available. (Rephrased from a follow-up.)
Must not: return a broken URL.

reply.answer:
Subtype is patient-level; join via patient.Yes, 7p copy number differs a lot between the three TCGA lower grade glioma (LGG) molecular subtypes. Gain of 7p is far more common in IDH-wildtype tumors than in either IDH-mutant subtype. I haven't run a statistical test, so I can't give a p-value.

**Cohort:** Brain Lower Grade Glioma (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas), using the arm-level copy number calls for 7p. Counts are per patient.

| Subtype | 7p gain | 7p unchanged | 7p loss | Not available | % with gain (of profiled) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| IDH-wildtype | 59 | 30 | 0 | 3 | 59/89 (66.3%) |
| IDH-mutant, non-codeleted | 29 | 214 | 0 | 5 | 29/243 (11.9%) |
| IDH-mutant, 1p/19q-codeleted | 8 | 156 | 0 | 3 | 8/164 (4.9%) |

- **Direction of the difference:** 7p gain is the dominant event in IDH-wildtype tumors. It is uncommon in the non-codeleted subtype and rarer still in the codeleted subtype.
- **No 7p loss:** no patient in any subtype has a 7p loss call.
- **Missing subtype:** 7 patients have no subtype label (3 unchanged, 4 not available) and are excluded from the table.
- **Percentages:** they use only patients with a 7p call, so the "not available" patients are left out of the denominator.

**Statistical test:** the right test for this 3-group by gain/no-gain table is a chi-squared test, and the expected cell counts are large enough for it to be reliable. You can run it in the comparison link below or in R with `chisq.test()`. If you test several chromosome arms at once, apply a Benjamini-Hochberg correction.

[Open the arm-level copy number comparison across the three subtypes](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/generic_assay_armlevel_cna?comparisonId=6b06da6bf66565fdc7916acb)

This page ranks chromosome arms by how much their gain and loss frequencies differ across the groups. It includes the test statistics for 7p. The groups are IDH-wildtype (92 samples), IDH-mutant codeleted (167) and IDH-mutant non-codeleted (248). Those sample counts include samples without a 7p call, so they are larger than the profiled counts above.

You can also explore each group in the [study view](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018). The older TCGA Firehose Legacy LGG study (`lgg_tcga`) has no arm-level copy number data.

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_metabric'
ORDER BY profile_type;
```

Common values across the public portal:

| Family | Profile types |
|---|---|
| mRNA expression | `rna_seq_v2_mrna`, `rna_seq_v2_mrna_median_Zscores`, `rna_seq_v2_mrna_median_all_sample_Zscores` (TCGA Pan … (6431 more chars)

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. # Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. # Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

```sql
-- Get clinical data for specific attributes
SELECT
    sample_unique_id,
    patient_unique_id,
    attribute_name,
    attribute_value
FROM clinical_data_derived

reply.answer:
I used the TCGA PanCancer Atlas lower grade glioma study (514 samples). In that study, 87 samples have a copy-number gain of EGFR. GISTIC calls these "Gained", which is a low-level gain and is not the same as amplification.

| EGFR copy-number call | Samples |
|---|---|
| Heterozygous deletion | 4 |
| Diploid | 381 |
| **Gain** | **87** |
| Amplification | 39 |
| Not available | 3 |

- [Study View filtered to EGFR gain](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018#filterJson=%7B%22genomicDataFilters%22%3A%5B%7B%22hugoGeneSymbol%22%3A%22EGFR%22%2C%22profileType%22%3A%22gistic%22%2C%22values%22%3A%5B%7B%22value%22%3A%221%22%7D%5D%7D%5D%7D) shows the 87 samples with clinical and genomic summaries. You can open the sample list from there.
- [OncoPrint for EGFR: GAIN](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/oncoprint?cancer_study_list=lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&gene_list=EGFR%3A+GAIN&case_set_id=lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018_all) shows the gains sample by sample across the whole cohort.

The Study View link filters to gain only. The 39 amplified samples are excluded.

There is also an older study, [Brain Lower Grade Glioma (TCGA, Firehose Legacy)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=lgg_tcga), with 530 samples. I haven't checked its EGFR counts.

question.question: is there a relationship between cic mutation and 19q del in lgg?
question.notes:
A correct answer must: link directly to the group comparison arm-level CNA subtab for CIC-mutant vs other samples, where 19q deletion is shown.
Must not: tell the user to look for 19q genes manually in the enrichment table.

reply.answer:
Yes, the counts in TCGA LGG (PanCancer Atlas) show a strong association. I can't give you a p-value, because I can't run statistical tests. The link below runs the test in cBioPortal.

**Counts (samples, mutation-profiled, with an arm-level 19q call; 440 samples)**

| | 19q loss | No 19q loss (unchanged or gain) | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CIC-mutant** | 104 (99.0%) | 1 (1.0%) | 105 |
| **CIC wild-type** | 81 (24.2%) | 254 (75.8%) | 335 |

- The 74 samples with no 19q call (3 CIC-mutant, 71 wild-type) are left out of the table.
- The cohort is 514 samples, 108 of them CIC-mutant.
- Of the 105 CIC-mutant samples with a 19q call, 104 have 19q loss. The one exception is 19q "unchanged".
- Among wild-type samples, 19 have 19q gain, 235 are unchanged, and 81 have loss.
- 19q loss is also common without a CIC mutation (81 samples), so CIC mutation isn't required for it.
- These counts show the direction and size of the association, but they don't establish significance.

**Test to run:** a 2×2 Fisher's exact test (two-tailed). One cell has a count of 1, so Fisher's is the right choice over chi-squared.
- **R:** `fisher.test(matrix(c(104, 81, 1, 254), nrow=2))`
- **Python:** `scipy.stats.fisher_exact([[104, 1], [81, 254]])`

**In cBioPortal:** [CIC-mutant vs wild-type: arm-level CNA enrichment](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/generic_assay_armlevel_cna?comparisonId=6b06da8a90693c4391916acc) shows 19q alongside the other chromosome arms, with statistics. The wild-type group includes only mutation-profiled samples. Here is the [study view for this cohort](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018#filterJson=%7B%22genomicProfiles%22%3A%5B%5B%22mutations%22%5D%5D%7D).

The 19q call comes from the study's arm-level copy-number annotation, not from a gene-level CNA call.

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_metabric'
ORDER BY profile_type;
```

| Family | Profile types |

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.

reply.answer:
**Cohort:** Brain Lower Grade Glioma (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas), `lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018`. It has 514 samples, and 511 of them are profiled for both mutations and copy number. I counted samples.

| Group | Samples |
|---|---|
| TP53 mutant | 249 |
| EGFR amplified (GISTIC +2) | 39 |
| Both TP53 mutant and EGFR amplified | 6 |
| **TP53 mutant or EGFR amplified** | **282** (about 55% of the 511 profiled) |

**Links**
- [OncoPrint of TP53 mutations and EGFR amplifications](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/oncoprint?cancer_study_list=lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&gene_list=TP53%3A+MUT%0AEGFR%3A+AMP&case_set_id=lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018_all). This is the one view that shows both conditions together, with one row per sample.
- [TP53-mutant samples in Study View](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018#filterJson=%7B%22geneFilters%22%3A%5B%7B%22geneQueries%22%3A%5B%5B%7B%22hugoGeneSymbol%22%3A%22TP53%22%7D%5D%5D%2C%22molecularProfileIds%22%3A%5B%22lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018_mutations%22%5D%7D%5D%7D)
- [EGFR-amplified samples in Study View](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018#filterJson=%7B%22geneFilters%22%3A%5B%7B%22geneQueries%22%3A%5B%5B%7B%22alterations%22%3A%5B%22AMP%22%5D%2C%22hugoGeneSymbol%22%3A%22EGFR%22%7D%5D%5D%2C%22molecularProfileIds%22%3A%5B%22lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018_gistic%22%5D%7D%5D%7D)

Study View can't filter on mutation OR amplification in one step, because the two come from different data types. To get one combined sample list from the two Study View links:
1. Open the first link, click **Custom Selection**, and then click **currently selected** to fill the text box with those sample IDs. Copy the list.
2. Open the second link and click **Custom Selection**. Paste in the copied IDs, then click **Filter to listed samples**.

**Alternative cohort:** [Brain Lower Grade Glioma (TCGA, Firehose Legacy)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=lgg_tcga) has 530 samples, if you want that version.

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.
- **For "across cancer types" questions**, jump to the [Cross-Cancer-Type Mutation Frequency](#cross-cancer-type-mutation-frequency) section below — there is one correct recipe and several common wrong ones.

## Counting Unit: Samples vs Patients

Before answering any mutation count or frequency question, decide whether the unit is samples or patients and state that choice in the answer.

| User wording | Counting unit |
|--------------|---------------|
| "prevalence", "rate", "fraction of patients", "patients with", "how common is" | Patient-level: `COUNT(DISTINCT patient_unique_id)` |
| "samples", "s … (37988 more chars)

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

reply.answer:
I filtered the TCGA Cell 2013 glioblastoma study to MGMT-methylated tumors. I used this study because it's the only TCGA GBM cohort here with a ready-made MGMT methylation call.

[View GBM with MGMT methylation (TCGA, Cell 2013)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=gbm_tcga_pub2013#filterJson=%7B%22clinicalDataFilters%22%3A%5B%7B%22attributeId%22%3A%22MGMT_STATUS%22%2C%22values%22%3A%5B%7B%22value%22%3A%22METHYLATED%22%7D%5D%7D%5D%7D)

**MGMT status in this cohort (577 samples):**
- Methylated: 170 (about 29% of all samples, or 49% of the 350 with a call)
- Unmethylated: 180
- No call: 227

Other TCGA GBM cohorts have methylation data but no MGMT status call. They include [GBM PanCancer Atlas](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=gbm_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018), [GBM Firehose Legacy](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=gbm_tcga) and [GBM Nature 2008](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=gbm_tcga_pub). question.question: show me point mutations in EGFR in lung cancer
question.notes:
A correct answer must: return a working link (after choosing or stating a study, e.g. luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018), treating point mutations as all SNVs rather than only missense.
Must not: return a blank response.

reply.answer:
I read "point mutations" as single-nucleotide changes, which is mostly missense. "Point mutation" can also include nonsense and splice-site changes, so the table below shows every mutation type. Tell me if you want a narrower definition.

I used the two TCGA PanCancer Atlas lung cohorts, counting samples. Each sample is counted once per mutation type, so a sample with two types appears in both rows.

**Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD)**, 566 profiled samples

| Mutation type | Samples | Distinct protein changes |
|---|---|---|
| Missense | 53 (9.4%) | 25 |
| In-frame deletion | 26 (4.6%) | 7 |
| In-frame insertion | 3 (0.5%) | 3 |
| Nonsense | 2 (0.4%) | 2 |
| Frame-shift deletion | 1 (0.2%) | 1 |
| Splice region | 1 (0.2%) | 1 |

The most common missense changes in LUAD are:
- L858R: 23 samples (4.1%)
- L861Q: 3 samples
- S768I, T790M, G719A and L62R: 2 samples each

| Missense | 10 (2.1%) | 9 |
| Splice region | 2 (0.4%) | 2 |

This guide highlights frequent mistakes when analyzing cBioPortal data and provides solutions to avoid them.

## Critical Pitfalls

### 1. 🚨 CRITICAL MUTATION FREQUENCY ERRORS

#### ❌ WRONG: Using study-wide totals for gene frequencies
```sql

    hugo_gene_symbol,

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.
- **For "across cancer types" questions**, jump to the [Cross-Cancer-Type Mutation Frequency](#cross-cancer-type-mutation-frequency) section below — there is one correct recipe and several common wrong ones.

reply.answer:
EGFR mRNA expression is highest in glioblastoma and falls to near zero in leukemia.

I used the 32 TCGA PanCancer Atlas cohorts, which were batch-normalized together, so the values can be compared across cancer types. Expression is log2(RSEM + 1), counted per sample. Z-scores wouldn't work here, because they're centered within each study and hide differences between cancer types.

I've listed the top 12 cancer types by 90th percentile below. I included that percentile because EGFR amplification in a subset of tumors shows up in the upper tail, not the median.

| Cancer type | Samples | Median | 90th percentile |
|---|---|---|---|
| Glioblastoma | 160 | 11.93 | 15.00 |
| Glioma (lower grade) | 514 | 11.24 | 13.05 |
| Head and Neck Cancer | 515 | 11.50 | 12.98 |
| Renal Clear Cell Carcinoma | 510 | 11.28 | 12.54 |
| Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer | 994 | 10.49 | 12.05 |
| Esophagogastric Cancer | 593 | 9.60 | 11.70 |
| Bladder Cancer | 407 | 9.27 | 11.45 |
| Pleural Mesothelioma | 87 | 9.75 | 11.33 |
| Cervical Cancer | 294 | 9.71 | 11.32 |
| Hepatobiliary Cancer | 366 | 9.67 | 11.22 |
| Renal Non-Clear Cell Carcinoma | 348 | 9.41 | 11.03 |
| Thyroid Cancer | 498 | 9.61 | 10.96 |

- **Highest:** Glioblastoma has the highest 90th percentile (15.00). Its median (11.93) is also the highest. The gap between its median and its 90th percentile is wider than for any other cancer type in the list, so it has a high-expressing tail. The values are consistent with the amplification you'd expect in a subset of these tumors, but I didn't check copy number here.
- **Intermediate:** Breast cancer has a median of 7.39 and a 90th percentile of 9.76. Ovarian epithelial tumors have a median of 7.76 and a 90th percentile of 9.02.
- **Lowest:** Melanoma has a median of 4.85, and mature B-cell neoplasms 4.25. Leukemia has a median of −0.10, which is essentially no expression.

Sample counts are TCGA samples, and a few cohorts overlap, such as glioma and glioblastoma, so don't add the totals together.

[View the EGFR expression plot by cancer type in cBioPortal](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/plots?cancer_study_list=acc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cblca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cbrca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ccesc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cchol_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ccoadread_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cdlbc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cesca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cgbm_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Chnsc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ckich_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ckirc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ckirp_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Claml_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Clgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Clihc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cluad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Clusc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cmeso_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cov_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cpaad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cpcpg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cprad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Csarc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cskcm_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cstad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Ctgct_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cthca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cthym_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cucec_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cucs_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cuvm_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&gene_list=EGFR&case_set_id=all&plots_horz_selection=%7B%22dataType%22%3A%22clinical_attribute%22%2C%22selectedDataSourceOption%22%3A%22CANCER_TYPE%22%7D&plots_vert_selection=%7B%22selectedGeneOption%22%3A%221956%22%2C%22dataType%22%3A%22MRNA_EXPRESSION%22%2C%22selectedDataSourceOption%22%3A%22rna_seq_v2_mrna%22%2C%22logScale%22%3A%22true%22%7D)
